#6309. Chocolate-Covered Caramel Apple Slices Are the Easiest Treats for Fall Get-Togethers

These chocolate-covered caramel apple slices turn the fruit into a glorified candy bar. Bring them to Friendsgiving or keep them in the fridge for a quick weekday snack.

With two little girls who have been loving all things fall these past couple months, my social algorithm has been filled with cozy crafts, Halloween costume ideas, and, of course, all the seasonal treats. When I scrolled to these chocolate-covered apple slices on a stick from @Crowded kitchen, I knew my daughters would go crazy for them.

Whole, uncut candy-coated apples are too big and too difficult for them to eat, but their eyes widen with delight every time we see them in the store. That’s exactly why this tip is genius. All the chocolate, caramel and fun toppings of a whole apple, but served in easy-to-enjoy slices. My girls loved decorating these treats as much as they loved eating them.

And to be honest, even though they’re easy for kids, they’re easier for adults just the same! Plus, the slices are shareable. This format makes them ideal if you’re looking for simple Friendsgiving ideas or low-lift Thanksgiving desserts.

You’ll start by cutting 1/2-inch thick slices from a whole apple. I like to trim the curviest part first and leave it for a snack, while focusing on the broader part of the apple for the slices. You will also need to strategically work around the core and pick out any seeds before proceeding. From there, you can either insert a candy stick or simply use a bamboo skewer, as I did here.

For the chocolate coating, I prefer to use almond bark chocolate coating instead of traditional chocolate bars or chips. It melts more smoothly and sets quickly without the fussy tempering required for real chocolate.

Cut the apples lengthwise into 1/2-inch thick slices. Insert a stick or skewer into one end of each slice. Cover a baking sheet in parchment, and set aside.

In a microwave-safe bowl, heat the almond bark in 30-second intervals until melted, stirring after each interval.

Spoon the melted chocolate coating over the apple slices, and place them on the prepared baking sheet.

Decorate each chocolate apple slice as desired. Allow the chocolate coating to firm up and set at room temperature before enjoying.

I love serving these candy caramel apple slices on a stick because it makes them so easy to eat. My girls loved them because it’s like having giant, fancy lollipops. You can use either a candy stick (you might be able to find them in the baking section of grocery stores) or a bamboo skewer. Candy sticks might not be as readily available, but they are sturdier. Bamboo skewers are effortless to insert and easy to find, but they are a little flimsier, and you have to be careful not to poke yourself while eating the apple.

What candy combo would you make? Let us know in the comments below!

#6308. Ocean Spray Just Gave Canned Cranberry Sauce A Chocolate Makeover

Someone finally saw the potential in those jiggly, ridged slices.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Canned cranberry sauce has some pretty stiff competition at Thanksgiving. Between the mashed potatoes, stuffing, and mac and cheese, that jiggly little side dish often gets treated like the ugly stepsister of the dinner table. And it probably doesn't help that it comes out looking exactly like the can it was packaged in.

But perhaps a little chocolate could improve its reputation.

Ocean Spray and Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés have teamed up with recipe developer Carolina Gelen on a new treat called Chocolate Covered Cranberry Sauce, taking the familiar Ocean Spray stuff and turning it into chocolate-coated discs, sold in packs of four.

If that sounds vaguely familiar, you may have seen Gelen's original Instagram video from 2023, when she experimented with dipping slices of canned cranberry sauce in chocolate (the recipe has since racked up more than 10 million views).

Ocean Spray's Kelvin Vuong said Gelen's recipe was exactly the kind of unexpected use for cranberry sauce the company wanted to share with more people. The brand eventually partnered with her and Compartés to turn the homemade recipe into something people could purchase—and Gelen is pretty thrilled to see her original experiment come this far.

"Getting to work with Ocean Spray and Compartés to turn that idea into something people across the country can try is incredibly exciting," she said in the announcement.

As for why this combination works, Compartés' creative director and chief chocolatier, Jonathan Grahm, pointed to the contrast between the cranberries' sharp, sour flavor and the richness of the chocolate. It's the same reason tart fruit and chocolate can work so well together, even if cranberry sauce isn't exactly the first thing you'd think to dip.

The limited-edition chocolates are available exclusively at Compartés for $24.95 per four-pack, while supplies last, with the gourmet chocolate brand also making chocolate turkeys filled with Ocean Spray's whole-berry cranberry sauce in both milk and dark chocolate options.

Cranberry sauce might never get the same love as mashed potatoes, but chocolate certainly gives it a fighting chance.

#6307. The Comfy Pants BA Editors Are Wearing to Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is my favorite holiday, not an uncommon feeling around the BA offices. I love the planning, the days (yes: days plural) spent preparing the feast in the kitchen alongside my mom, the gathering of loved ones around a table to reflect, savor, and enjoy. There is one thing, however, that I don’t love: The moment after dinner and before dessert in which I become so full that I must excuse myself and retire to the couch, where I clutch a pillow to my stomach until I’ve digested enough to reemerge.

As somewhat of an expert in feeling Too Full and Bloated™, I can attest that this feeling is made infinitely worse when I’m wearing rigid, tight-waisted pants. Perhaps you can relate? While stretchy sweatpants are an obvious solution here, there are only so many meal scenarios in which it’s socially acceptable to wear them. For those other occasions—the holiday feasts, celebratory meals out, and thousand-course tasting menu dinners—I’ve made it my mission to fill my wardrobe with pants that look polished and feel comfortable, no matter how many helpings of stuffing or “fries for the table” I’ve had. Here are my tried-and-true favorite pairs for eating big meals in, along with my fellow food-loving colleagues’ go-tos.

I was a die-hard high-waist pants gal for the majority of my life. Then I tried Still Here’s Everyday Jeans. A true mid-rise, they hit just above my hip bones and about an inch below my belly button, hugging my body without digging in, even after a holiday dinner or multicourse restaurant meal. The non-stretch denim is soft but sturdy, and the relaxed leg is structured without feeling at all rigid. I own them in Washed Black and Classic Blue and wear them constantly, to everything from casual weeknight dinners (paired with sneakers and a white tee) to weekend date nights (with kitten heels and a silk top). They’ve even become my go-to Friendsgiving uniform in recent years because of how comfortable they are to cook, eat, and host in.

If you haven’t already heard of Rag & Bone’s Miramar line, let me put you on: These pants look like real denim, but are actually made from soft cotton terry. It’s all thanks to the brand’s printing technique, which allows them to digitally print details like weave, stitching, buttons, and pockets onto any fabric. Ever since I got my first pair, I’ve been delighted every time I receive a compliment on my jeans and can reveal that they’re actually—gasp—sweatpants! I’ve owned the Sofie style for a few years now, which have real pockets and a true button fly that give them a more polished look; but my recent obsession are the Sport Stripe Track Pants, which have a flattering wide-leg cut and a fully elastic waistband that makes them ideal for multicourse meals.

I invested in a pair of poplin pants from Suzie Kondi this summer and they’ve quickly become my go-to attire whenever I want the comfort of an elastic waistband while still looking put-together. The low-rise waist sits comfortably on my hips and ensures that nothing squeezes my midsection, and the straight leg cut is incredibly flattering. The cotton poplin fabric is breathable and feels quite luxe, and I’ve even noticed that stains come out surprisingly easily (which I learned the hard way by spilling green juice all over myself testing personal blenders). Forever a fan of a monochrome ’fit, I love pairing mine with the matching Vella shirt.

If you’re looking for a more affordable option, J.Crew’s Luna Pants have gained a well-deserved following on social media this year. They’re just as stylish as the pricier brands, available in several colors, and ring in at under $100.

Many of the above pants feel like sweatpants, but if you’re enjoying a casual dinner, there’s nothing stopping you from wearing actual sweatpants—particularly if you opt for an elevated pair that ditches the typical brushed fleece for cashmere or velour in a straight-leg cut. Senior reviews editor Olivia Tarantino and I are both fans of Quince’s Mongolian Cashmere Straight Leg Pants for their ultrasoft feel and flattering cut. If you’re looking to upgrade to something more luxe, executive audience development director Casey Hendricks vouches for the cashmere Everywhere Pant from Guest in Residence: “They’re THE pants for when you can’t fathom wearing actual pants. They’re comfortable but structured for sweatpants, and they’re super warm. I’ve had these pants for years and they still feel and look good as new.” I’m also partial to Suzie Kondi’s Lito Pants, which are cut from cozy velour and have a slightly flared leg that looks good on everyone. While I don’t own these myself, I steal my mom’s pair every time I’m home to visit (sorry, Mom!).

100% Washable Silk Drawstring Wide Leg Pants

For dressier dinners, I like to opt for a pair of slinky satin pants. The elastic waistband and flowy fabric ensures they stay comfy even after the meal is said and done, while the shine and elegant drape make them easy to dress up. Hendricks calls La Ligne’s Colby Pants her “everything pants.” She says she wears them for “work, errands, eating, airport, and everything in between. They’re so comfortable but also so chic—they make me feel effortlessly put-together.” I also love Quince’s 100% Washable Silk Drawstring Wide Leg Pants, which have an impressive sub-$100 price tag and are (as the name suggests) magically machine washable.

Long gone are the days where I’ve been an athleisure-on-the-plane kind of girl. In this job (and in life in general), I've started to prefer clothes that are both comfortable and acceptable to wear to a restaurant meal straight from the plane. Enter the Reformation Olina Linen Pants. They’re perhaps the only pants that I’d wear on an 11-hour travel day straight into a few-hours-long dinner, and in fact, I have. The linen gives them an elevated look, but the drawstring waist and just-soft-enough fabric make them easy to sit in for a long while. I’m tempted to order them in every color, but my singular pair has lasted many trips, many meals, and many washes thus far. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

As an adult man approaching 40, I want a pair of pants just wide enough to convey I’m in the know without going full MC Hammer. Enter the Uniqlo pleated, relaxed wide pants. With an elastic, drawstring waistband and belt loops, I get to dine out free from navel constrictions and still wear a smart belt. I can go from the office to the bistro to the couch without sacrificing comfort or functionality. To you, the casual observer, though, I look like I’m wearing slacks. With the loose, high-waist fit, these pants drape beautifully with a pair of black leather penny loafers. They’re made of 67% recycled polyester, which feels virtuous and breezy. —Gabe Hiatt, senior restaurants editor

I am content with my daily uniform of selvedge jeans, leather shoes, and a dark T-shirt or sweater depending on the weather. It’s not too formal for working in a kitchen, but acceptable should I find myself in an elevator with someone from Vogue. But running around town all day, with the occasional epic dinner out, means a constant trade-off between style and comfort. Whoever designed 100% cotton jeans for railroad workers and miners just didn’t consider the rigors of a 3-hour meal followed by a long train ride home. So lately I have been quietly upgrading my look with Naked and Famous Denim’s stretch selvedge jeans. They contain 2% elastane (perhaps you know it as Spandex), just enough to provide a forgiving fit, but with the look and patina of raw denim. They stay conformable enough all day that you can simply ignore them and think about more important things: like dinner. —Chris Morocco, food director

There is no worse feeling than the cold, hard button of a stiff jean pressing against your full stomach after a particularly big meal. (Who designed jeans anyway?). That’s why for Thanksgiving there won’t be a firm, oppressive waistband in sight. I already know I’ll be donning my Le Bon Shoppe Arc Pants, not only for their loose barrel-leg silhouette, but also for their forgiving elasticated waist band. Namely, more pie for me, without the feeling of “pants” up against my indulgent belly. Pair with a festive cashmere sweater (preferably oversized) and you can go from the dinner table straight to the couch for your turkey-induced coma in both style and comfort. —June Kim, executive editor

As someone who’s no stranger to a mid-meal top-button release, I’ve developed a deep appreciation for an elastic waistband. Even better when it comes in a pair of pants I’m excited to wear. My current favorite: J.Crew’s Luna pants in lightweight corduroy. A more fall-friendly take on the poplin version above, these are like sweatpants disguised as corduroys, with plenty of room for big Thanksgiving ambitions while still making you feel put-together. Honestly, what more could you ask of a pant?

You can dress them up with a sweater and loafers or keep it casual with a T-shirt and sneakers. I’ve worn them so often that I’m already plotting a second pair in a different color. My one caveat: They tend to run a little big, so I’d suggest sizing down. —Gabby Fowler, social media director

#6306. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

#6305. All The Avengers: Doomsday Food Collabs You Can Get Your Hands On Right Now

My bank account might not survive this movie.

Doctor Doom hasn't even arrived in theaters yet, and Avengers: Doomsday is already taking over just about everything I eat and drink.

I've talked about being a die-hard Marvel fan before, but this is one movie where you can pretty much guarantee I'll be ordering every themed drink, trying every snack, and buying every collectible I can get my hands on. And if some of those purchases happen to find their way into the movie theater with me on December 17, well, I won't tell if you won't. (Sorry, AMC.)

With the film officially opening next month, restaurants and food brands have been busy giving us plenty of ways to spend our money before we've even bought a ticket. So whether you're a fellow Marvel obsessive or just someone who could use an excuse to order more donuts, here's a look at the Avengers: Doomsday food and drink collaborations you can find stateside.

Dunkin's massive Marvel collaboration launched November 4 with six themed drinks, including the Iced Captain'ccino, Doom Cloud Latte, and Wakandan Daydream Refresher, along with special donuts and MUNCHKINS. As if the drinks weren't enough to drain your wallet, collectible tumblers, mugs, cup sleeves, and even a Doctor Doom MUNCHKINS tin are also available to add to your collection. And if you happen to live in New York, Boston, Chicago, or Los Angeles, four Dunkin' restaurants are getting full Marvel makeovers beginning November 17.

Jack in the Box is feeding the entire team with its Doomsday Dipping Box, which packs popcorn chicken, mozzarella sticks, tacos, curly fries, a drink, and three dipping sauces—including the mysterious Assemble Sauce—into one meal. Available since November 5, the meal also comes with one of eight surprise magnets that fit together like puzzle pieces. If you're determined to collect the entire set, I hope you really like curly fries.

Dave & Buster's is committed to the superhero bit, going so far as to temporarily rename itself Doom & Buster's when the nationwide takeover officially begins November 16. It’ll bring Marvel-themed arcade experiences, prizes, collectible Power Cards, and five specialty drinks, including the Panther's Potion and Captain Punch mocktails. There's also DOOMHOUR, when rewards members can earn double tickets on eligible games during surprise one-hour windows, with the promotion running through January 31, 2027.

Considering Robert Downey Jr. co-founded happy coffee and is playing Doctor Doom, this partnership practically wrote itself. The brand has released eight collectible Marvel cans across four drinks: Classic Cold Brew, Tahitian Vanilla Cold Brew, Vanilla Latte, and Chocolatey Chip Latte. Each flavor features two character designs, including Doctor Doom, Thor, Gambit, and Mystique, and they're available online and at select retailers nationwide.

Even the M&M's characters are getting suited up. The candy brand has released special Marvel packages featuring combinations like Red as Deadpool, Blue as Daredevil, and Green as She-Hulk, plus a Walmart-exclusive design starring Yellow dressed as Doctor Doom. There's no new candy flavor involved, but you can enter a sweepstakes for prizes including a Disney Cruise Line vacation, and there's even a Marvel crossover comic book.

No new popcorn flavor here, but Pop Secret is giving several of its existing varieties special Avengers: Doomsday packaging with a pretty convenient offer. If you buy three qualifying Pop Secret products in one purchase and submit your receipt, you can get a Fandango code worth $8 off admission. There's also a sweepstakes offering a trip to New York City and a few other prizes, so if you’re already assembling this many movie snacks, you might as well save a few bucks on the ticket.

#6304. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6302. 31 Thanksgiving Pies Worth a Second Slice at Breakfast

Some people will happily eat a slice of cheesecake after Thanksgiving dinner. We respect that. But this list of Thanksgiving pie recipes is for those of us who already have our forks poised over the pie table, whipped cream at the ready.

You’ll find the classics: silky pumpkin pie, gooey pecan pie, and apple pie with a double crust and another with cinnamon crumble. Then things get interesting: cranberry meringue with lime-sharpened curd, butterscotch custard with a blanket of toasted marshmallow, a pecan cream pie that doesn’t know when to stop layering. We’ve also got chilled chocolate pies, citrusy custards, and more than a few excellent candidates for breakfast the next morning.

Need more inspiration? Browse our favorite pie recipes or the rest of our Thanksgiving desserts. For help with the pastry, check out our guide to making better pie or the best store-bought pie crusts.

Silky pumpkin custard, a buttery, flaky crust, and just the right amount of warming spice. Maple syrup and vanilla bring extra depth to this Thanksgiving classic, which has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics.

A beautiful lattice crust is just the introduction. Beneath it, Honeycrisp apples meet smoky burnt-sugar caramel and a generous pour of bourbon. Give this pie plenty of time to cool before slicing.

“This old Gramma has been baking pies for MANY years and this is by far the best pecan pie recipe I have ever used,” wrote one of our readers. Gramma from Chattanooga, Tennessee, we salute you.

That crimson cranberry-lime curd is as tart and punchy as it looks; a billowing meringue cap supplies the sweetness. Start the day before serving so the filling has ample time to set.

Claire Saffitz’s deep-dish apple pie builds flavor with reduced cider, vanilla, and cardamom. Sweet-tart Pink Ladies are our first choice for the filling, but plenty of other excellent baking apples work.

If pecan pie and cream pie had a very ambitious child, this would be it. A nut-packed base, brown sugar custard, tangy whipped cream, and candied pecans make each slice a four-layer event.

Detroit’s Sister Pie brings the drama with a flaky crust, dark chocolate ganache, salty-sweet butterscotch custard, and a homemade marshmallow topping toasted to golden peaks. It’s a project, but what a payoff.

This classic Gourmet dessert makes a compelling case for ousting apples at Thanksgiving (jk, obviously you have to make both). Firm-ripe Anjou or Bartlett pears, a little nutmeg, and a flaky lattice crust are all it takes.

Fresh ginger and a trio of warming spices bring depth to the sweet potato custard. The coup de grâce: a cloud of marshmallow-spiked whipped cream that gives sweet potato casserole some dessert-table competition.

The lemon filling means business—it gets the zest of four whole lemons. A towering crown of toasted meringue brings the drama, but you can break up the work over a few days.

For anyone who prefers streusel to a pastry lattice, this is your pie. A thick layer of cinnamon-spiced apples settles beneath a buttery crumb topping. A scoop of vanilla ice cream is highly encouraged.

Alison Roman’s Southern-style custard pie brings lemon zest, tangy buttermilk, and optional saffron to a tender, flaky crust. The saffron adds a delicate floral note and gives the filling its golden glow.

Inspired by the author’s Filipino family holiday traditions, this striking purple pie uses jarred ube halaya and coconut milk for a silky filling. A pearly marshmallow whip makes it look positively regal.

Think giant peanut butter cup + graham cracker crust. A fudgy chocolate layer sits beneath airy peanut butter mousse. This isn’t the time for drippy natural peanut butter; the conventional creamy stuff gives the filling its velvety texture.

Coffee ice cream, bourbon fudge, toasted pecans, and an Oreo crust make a gloriously rich frozen pie. Assemble it up to four days ahead and save that precious oven space for Thanksgiving dinner.

Maple syrup sweetens the warmly spiced pumpkin custard, while a toasty oat-flour crust makes this Gourmet adaptation a welcome gluten-free alternative. Use certified gluten-free oat flour and a labeled gluten-free flour blend.

This pecan pie’s dating app profile would read: “Gooey brown sugar filling, bittersweet chocolate throughout, cocoa crust, fluffy chocolate cream on top.” Are we swiping right? Obviously.

A tart, silky filling and billows of whipped cream make this pie a welcome break from all the brown sugar and spice. An egg yolk in the graham cracker crust helps it hold together for clean slices.

This Pennsylvania Dutch specialty is all about molasses: dark, sticky, and delicious beneath a crumbly topping that bakes into a striking marbled surface. A spoonful of whipped cream makes a fine companion.

What makes this British classic so brilliant? Instead of canned dulce de leche, we make a deep, chewy caramel sauce and add a layer of salted nuts. Bananas and whipped cream take it home.

Inspired by Greek bougatsa, this skillet-baked pie uses rumpled sheets of phyllo instead of traditional pastry. Don’t sweat the tears and folds; they’re what give the cinnamon-scented custard pie its dramatic, shatteringly crisp top.

A salty-sweet peanut-and-graham-cracker crust, banana-packed custard, and a mountain of whipped cream. The peanut topping makes this especially good for anyone who believes banana pudding could use a little crunch.

Imagine pumpkin pie with pecan pie’s best feature: that crunchy, candied nut topping. Now spike the custard with rye whiskey and deepen the crust’s flavor with rye flour. The best of both worlds, indeed.

This Southern specialty folds chocolate chips, bourbon, and your choice of pecans or walnuts into a gooey brown sugar filling. A generous pinch of salt keeps all that sweetness in check.

Before you ask: Yes, it’s dessert. No, there’s no chopped meat in this version. Instead, you get a glorious jumble of dried fruits, apples, warm spices, and rum tucked beneath a golden lattice crust. Prepare the filling at least 24 hours before assembly, or freeze it up to three months ahead.

Cherries at Thanksgiving? Absolutely, when you’re using frozen fruit. Almond flour makes the pastry especially tender, while lime zest brightens the tart cherry filling. A classic double-crust pie worth saving a slice of for breakfast.

#6301. Even for Desperate Restaurants, Fake Reviews Just Aren’t Worth It

A new report proves that planting fake Yelp reviews has dire long-term impacts on restaurants

When Yelp was first launched in 2004, it flopped. The company’s initial model of an email-based referral service failed to take off until its creators realized users were taking the platform into their own hands; in lieu of sending one another recommendations via email chain, they began using a “hidden” link at the bottom of the startup’s website to write unsolicited reviews of everything from doctors to restaurants. Yelp 2.0 launched in 2005, and gave those reviews a more visible place to live online — one that emboldened users to feel more authentic stewardship, by way of direct authorship, over hyping up the businesses they enjoyed (or didn’t). The startup bought a whopping 20-million-business database, and amplified a world of reviews outside of the restaurant- critic echo chamber. It was a fresh democratization of information, which was itself one of the more optimistic legacies of the Y2K internet.

It’s been over 20 years since Yelp was founded. At its best, the platform still feels like a place where the voices of hungry, curious diners can share their personal experiences and offer recommendations and tips; at its worst, it feels like a bloated repository for reviews filled with misdirected anger, unreasonable expectations, or else completely fake customer reviews. Initially, unsubstantiated and unreliable reviews were more often written by a person — either someone from the business itself, or paid by the business; now, a fake review can be penned by a paid influencer, a detailed generative AI prompt, or purchased from third-party agencies that will produce fake bot reviews in bulk.

Fake reviews were perhaps inevitable. Bot-driven comments became ubiquitous during an overripe moment in the untamed internet’s lifespan. But how does a restaurant shamed for gamifying its reviews — even if it was, presumably, out of desperation in a tough economic landscape — regain customers’ broken trust?

… The offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp.

In 2026’s AI-addled digital ecosystem, researchers are starting to understand even more about how paid-for, planted reviews impact the restaurants behind them, and whether trying to gamify platforms to achieve high ratings is worth it at all for businesses. A recently published working paper on the consequences of restaurants flagged by Yelp for fake (planted, incentivized) reviews found that since 2023, more than 4,900 businesses have been flagged with Yelp’s “Consumer Alert” banner, which exists on the penalized business’ page for a 90-day period and lets Yelp users know that the business has been caught peddling fake reviews. In 2020, the fast-casual chain Burgerim was found guilty of planting fake reviews, and received over 200 digital warning banners across its various locations’ Yelp pages.

The impacts of that digital pillory extend far beyond its 90-day duration. Yi Cao is an assistant professor of accounting at George Mason University, and the co-author of the paper; almost immediately, Cao noticed the offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp. Cao’s team cross-analyzed the business’ performance on Yelp with real-life foot traffic reports (from global location data firm SafeGraph) and credit card transaction data (courtesy of Consumer Edge), and discovered that most of the penalized restaurants struggled to recover to pre-alert traffic even after a year and a half. The stink of chicanery lingered.

While Cao says his team doesn’t know every signal that Yelp uses to identify fake reviews, they do know that it relies “substantially on reports from consumers and business owners,” and that “they also have an algorithm running in the background to screen reviews for AI-generated language — which is a sign of possible review inflation.” At this point, the cost of planting a good review is only getting steeper as the technology capable of detecting it improves. “This is a classical theory of a trade-off between the benefits of manipulating reputation and the risks of getting caught,” Cao explains, “When the risk is relatively low, the business owners decide the incremental benefits are worth the risk.”

Yelp’s real restaurant reviews don’t necessarily need to be etched in stone, but as AI-penned reviews become less detectable and more sophisticated, what diners want now, more than ever, is a human touch and a sense of authenticity.

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

Multiple simulated spaceflight stressors impact cardiac fibrosis, calcium dynamics, immune function, cytokines and gene variants in rat, Rattus norvegicus. Her work has appeared in outlets such as Nature, SELF, and The Transmitter.

#6298. Food-Themed Fashion Is Starting to Feel Gluttonous

﻿The millennial avocado obsession walked so the Loewe tomato clutch could run

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

There was a time, not too long ago, when a purse shaped like a baguette felt like a thrilling — even subversive — novelty. Now, we hardly bat an eye when we see that Moschino has made a trompe l’oeil celery purse, or that Big Bud Press is making a hot-dog-and-pretzel-print jumpsuit in collaboration with a Los Angeles bar. How did we get here? And has it all become a little too much?

Fashion has long found inspiration from the culinary world, but the influx of food-fueled prints, graphics, and trompe l’oeil accessories that picked up steam during the pandemic have now reached a cultural tipping point.

The then-emerging brand made food a central theme of its vision: Its cake-topped aviator caps, Ferrero Rocher heels, and beeswax-sculpted cheese hats — hyperrealistic, absurdist food designs capable of achieving instant social media virality. Prior to working in fashion, Puppets designer Carly Mark was working as an artist whose pieces revolved around candies and snacks. As she told Business of Fashion in 2023, the Puppets universe felt like the ideal pairing given what she considers food and fashion’s motivators: pleasure and money.

During the pandemic, the much-duped “strawberry dress” took over TikTok, and Tombolo Company found a hit on its hands with its vongole shirt, which debuted in 2019, but found peak popularity in 2021. The shirt appeared in Vogue in 2020, and InsideHook called it an “obvious bedfellow to day-drinks, rooftops and weekenders” — in other words, a status symbol. Katie Kimmel’s T-shirts made chicken-parm enthusiasm akin to being a devout sports fan, and in 2022, this very publication called “seafood kitsch” the look of the summer, as items like Rachel Antonoff’s super-popular seafood-tower dress flew off the digital shelves.

Why was food so primed to become a motif in clothing at this point in culture? One could make the argument that it has roots in the millennial optimism years: Earlier in the 2000s and 2010s, the concept of “foodies” was new. Brands printed tongue-in-cheek food- and coffee-related motifs and slogans (a fervent love of avocados comes to mind) on hipster apparel, as the idea that “you are what you eat” developed growing fervor. That period was a key stepping stone in the evolution toward the far more elaborate and pervasive marketability of food-as-identity we see today. Content creator Cole Poska, who is a partner and creative director at Beyond Studios, tells Eater that “food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.” Poska’s own Instagram often reimagines restaurant merch just for fun; his designs for Cheesecake Factory apparel went viral, such as a hat that resembles the iconic brown bread. He points out that people will defend their favorite fast-food order like it’s a family member, and with the kind of loyalty that’s hard to manufacture. The same could be said about their martini order, or favorite taco spot; it’s all a way of telling others who we are through what we like.

But the fatigue is undoubtedly here. In 2024, Bon Appétit asked “Why Does Every Dress Have Pasta and Cocktail Shrimp on It?” And as the novelty factor of a shrimp-print dress has worn off, the next question might be: Will there be any true longevity for these food-as-fashion moments? Our feeds overflow with products that are hurriedly designed for flash-in-the-pan viral trends and quickly destined for a landfill; arguably more so if the object in question prioritizes shock value and gimmicks over function and brand identity.

This is undoubtedly all related to the accelerated speed of trend cycles and shortened consumer attention spans. However, as Leah Asmelash wrote last year for CNN, the rising costs of food also casts an increasingly sinister shadow over food-themed fashion. In 2026, a $425 cardigan emblazoned with oysters has waning originality compared to a few years ago; it falls into banality at best and the Hunger Games at worst; its wearer indicating that they’re financially comfortable and, more importantly, well-fed. In that light, beyond its role in identity, food has become more of a status symbol than ever. A sweater touting one’s love of caviar is shorthand for their access to and appreciation of luxury, culinary and otherwise. But sporting the mass-market Temu version? It’s more akin to wearing a faux Gucci belt.

“Food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.”

If it’s possible to escape the sense of accelerated-trend-cycle disposability, it may have to be through a more subtle approach than, say, a bag that looks like a giant stick of butter. Sam Salad is the co-founder of Meals, a Los Angeles-based, workwear-inspired apparel company that, by its own description, “bakes ‘food culture’ into apparel, blurring the lines between the clothes we eat and the food we wear.” Utility is at the forefront of Meals, which offers a classic chef pant with a slightly fuller cut, in both basic colors and subdued aesthetic homages to blue cheese and watermelon. When Meals launched in 2019, Salad was selling premium denim along Venice’s Abbot Kinney Boulevard, a hotbed of Instagrammy food culture and trendy restaurants like Gjelina that helped inspire his own brand. “Design today has to translate across languages and platforms,” Salad tells Eater.

Food is hardly a new bedfellow for fashion designers, even if today’s hyper-fast trend cycle has kicked it into overdrive. “Food is totally universal,” Salad says. “Issey Miyake once merchandised their pleats collection as little omakase sets.” He cites that collection among other fashion-meets-food moments that he considers successful, such as the iconic Salvador Dalí- and Elsa Schiaparelli-designed lobster dress. At the time of its 1937 creation, the dress was a scandal: It assumed a conformity-defying sartorial stance and was fittingly worn by Wallace Simpson. Today, its highly devolved spawn are available on Shein for $13.

As it stands, one clear way out of corny, food motif purgatory is for brands — fashion or food — to focus less on quantity and more on storytelling and quality. “We do a few things really well, and that’s enough,” Salad says, “Like In-N-Out [Burger].”

Poska’s philosophy is similar. “I’d rather make one thing people talk about for a year than 20 things people forget about tomorrow,” he says. “The first person to make a candle look like a stick of butter is a genius. The hundredth person is just making a candle.”

#6297. 20 Food Advent Calendars to Buy Before They Sell Out (2026)

Nothing sparks joy and jumpstarts the Christmas season like a food advent calendar. You get 25 tiny compartments, each housing a festive treat hidden behind a perforated door. They’re not just chocolate anymore. These days, they’re filled with everything from gummies and chili crisp to whiskey and coffee. And if you’re thinking of ordering one to enjoy this year, the time is now. December 1st is only seven weeks away, and after reporting on these things for the past five years, we’ve seen these calendars sell out months in advance or get backordered every year.

The best advent calendars contain high-quality sweets, booze, condiments, snacks, teas, or coffees you’ll be genuinely excited to open every day. And who knows, they might even introduce you to a product you’ll want to buy on repeat once the holiday season has come and gone.

This list is filled with advent calendars for every type of food and beverage enthusiast, many of them from brands we’ve long known and loved: a chile crisp-filled calendar from Fly By Jing, a Bonne Maman calendar filled with mini jam jars, and a chocolate advent calendar for mythology heads from San Francisco-based Dandelion Chocolate. Pick one up for yourself, or snag a few to gift to friends in the lead-up to the holiday season. Order soon, though. These sell out well before December hits.

We try not to play favorites here at BA, but I’ll be honest: This is the advent calendar fellow commerce writer Wilder Davies and I most look forward to receiving every year. If you’ve never had Lakrids by Bülow, allow me to explain. Every perforated door reveals a pack (or four) of spherical licorice candies, each coated in a white or milk chocolate shell flavored with passion fruit, strawberries and cream, salted caramel—you get the idea. These candies are indescribably delicious and guaranteed to convert even the most staunch licorice haters.

If you, like me, are an absolute fiend for gummy candy, there’s no better advent calendar for you than Sockerbit’s. The New York-based Swedish candy company makes some of the tastiest gummies I’ve ever had, and their 25-day calendar features a selection of favorites from the brand’s vast catalogue. I won’t give the exact contents away, but know that the hefty box holds two pounds of gummies running the gamut from sour sugar-coated fruit slices to generously portioned colorful candy mixes.

This one’s for the chocolate lovers who appreciate a little mythology lesson, too. Hailing from San Francisco-based bean-to-bar chocolate maker Dandelion Chocolate, this advent calendar features handcrafted chocolates from 24 acclaimed chocolatiers, all of whom earned their spot through a series of blind tastings. Along with the chocolate (which is packaged in individual ornament boxes you can hang on your tree), you’ll receive an illustrated storybook full of tales adapted from Nordic mythology, a decorative keepsake star, and daily digital content to be enjoyed along with your treats.

If you’re looking for a fun, interactive take on the classic chocolate advent calendar, check out Delysia. The Austin-based chocolatier releases a new themed calendar every year that acts as a guessing game, with clues as to what each of the 25 truffle flavors is. This year’s edition is holiday movie-themed, and each chocolate corresponds to a classic festive film—think hot cocoa for The Polar Express, sesame praline and banana sour lime for The Grinch, and raspberry rose for It’s a Wonderful Life.

If you’ve got a hot chocolate lover in your life (or if that hot chocolate lover is you), this advent calendar from UK-based chocolatier Hotel Chocolat is the move. It contains 24 single-serve sachets of the brand’s signature velvety hot chocolate mix in a range of flavors, including some limited-edition seasonal varieties.

Venchi has been making chocolate in Italy for over 140 years, and its chocolates, bars, and gelatos can now be found in more than 70 countries across the globe. The brand’s Advent Calendar Deluxe Maxi would make a handsome gift for any chocolate lovers in your life who would appreciate a bit more variety than your standard selection of chocolate truffles. In addition to individually wrapped chocolates, this calendar also features bars, spreads, and small gift tins, so rest assured you’ll never be bored.

We’ve previously recommended the amaro from this Portland, Oregon-based craft cocktail brand, so it’s no surprise that they make a great advent calendar too. Straightaway’s 12 Nights of Cocktails calendar would be a welcome offering for any drinks lover in your life who’d appreciate the gift of 12 iconic cocktails, without the fuss of actually making them or acquiring all of the ingredients to do so. Each Straightaway cocktail is single-serve and ready to open, pour, and sip—no measuring required.

If you’ve ever dreamed of embarking on a month-long wine tasting, Vinebox’s wine advent calendars make that a reality. Choose between two 12-day options (“Vine” or “Velvet”), or opt for a 24-day set that includes both. The wines are sourced from all over the world, and each bottle contains 100 milliliters. If you’re curious to learn more about a particular variety, the advent calendar grants you access to sommelier-led virtual tasting videos to accompany each wine.

The Nespresso devotee in your life will delight at the chance to try a different classic or limited-edition coffee capsule every day in the lead-up to Christmas. This year’s calendars are part of the brand’s new collaboration with Swarovski and come in two versions, one for the original machine and one for the Vertuo. The last day contains a special gift, which I won’t spoil here.

Whiskey enthusiasts will love Flaviar’s luxe advent calendar, which includes 24 whiskies from all over the world, including pours from Japan, Ireland, and Finland. Along with the liquor, each kit comes with a set of two collectible Glencairn glasses, a free year of access to the brand’s Flaviar Black membership, and a tasting booklet with information on each variety and a QR code you can scan to learn more and purchase full bottles of anything you love.

Palais de Thés’s advent calendar makes our recommendation list year after year for a few reasons. For one, it’s beautiful and luxe-feeling while ringing in under $40. But the main reason is the quality and variety of what lies within each perforated door: an assortment of 24 tea bags that are, in commerce writer Wilder Davies’s words, “genuinely lovely.” Each calendar includes a mix of classics and more interesting festive blends far removed from the stereotypical holiday flavors that so easily stray into Bath and Body Works scented candle territory. Consider this the ultimate way to settle into cozy season.

Coffee purists will love every day of this advent calendar from Bean Box, made in collaboration with Onyx Coffee Lab. Each of the 24 days includes a signature blend or an exclusive Advent-only single-origin release, perfectly portioned for a 24-ounce pour-over.

There’s a chance you’ve seen this calendar from Bonne Maman on your Instagram feed, and we can confirm it’s worth the hype. The 24 mini jam jars are adorable, of course, but what we really love about this set is the unique flavors it includes—flavors like apricot lavender, cherry pink peppercorn, and raspberry lychee that you can't find in Bonne Maman’s regular lineup.

Tinned fish hive, rise up. This advent calendar from fan-favorite conservas brand Fishwife features 12 days’ worth of tasty tins and some exclusive fish-adjacent goodies. I won’t spoil exactly what’s in it, but know that some of our favorite offerings from the brand’s lineup include the Albacore Tuna with Spanish Lemon, Smoked Rainbow Trout with Red Chimichurri, and Smoked Salmon with Fly By Jing’s chili crisp.

12 days of cheese? Sign us up. This calendar from Murray’s Cheese sells out every year, so we’d recommend snagging one while you still can. It’s filled with a host of cheeses (like Parmigiano Reggiano, Gruyère, and truffle cheddar) and accoutrements (like apple butter and oat cakes) that you can fashion into a festive cheeseboard or enjoy one by one. And don’t worry, it arrives in an insulated shipper, but you do have to keep the whole calendar in the fridge throughout the holiday season.

2026 Limited Edition 12-Day Advent Calendar

2026 Limited Edition 24-Day Advent Calendar

Give the gift of 12 or 24 days of chile crisp and chile crisp-adjacent surprises with this advent calendar from one of our favorite spicy condiment brands. It contains an assortment of mini sauce jars, packs of the brand’s best-selling noodles, and some limited-edition surprises—so even if your pantry’s already stocked with Fly By Jing, you can find something new to love here. This calendar tends to sell out in October, so we’d recommend buying one soon.

This luxe advent calendar from Williams Sonoma has a little bit of everything. Balsamic vinegar from Modena? Check. A bundt pan-shaped ornament? Also check. This is the calendar to splurge on if you can’t decide whether you want chocolate or trinkets.

We all have that friend who seemingly can’t eat a meal without dousing it in hot sauce first. Get them this advent calendar from Uncommon Goods, which contains a mini bottle of hot sauce behind each of its 12 doors. These aren’t your average Cholulas or Tabascos. Instead, you’ll find flavors like Sweet Onion Habanero, Pineapple Papaya BBQ, Plum Reaper, and Psycho Curry, all ranging in spice level from sweet and mild to very hot.

#6296. The Next Ice Age Began 2,000 Years Ago. Then, in 1960, Humans Abruptly Ended It.

Ancient moss frozen beneath Baffin Island’s ice tells the story of a glaciation humans snuffed out.

Researchers at Columbia University have pinpointed the summer of 1960 as the moment when a new glacial period, which had already begun, started melting away. They said the blame rests squarely on humans and the surge in greenhouse gases.

In a new study published in the journal Science, the researchers wrote that the newest glacial period (often colloquially called an ice age) began 2,000 years ago, even though it would have taken about 30,000 years for anyone to really notice. Human activity cut it short in 1960.

“It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen—and yet it stopped,” Nicolas Young, a geochemist at the Columbia Climate School, said in a statement from Columbia University. “It’s a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.”

To gather their data, the team studied what remains of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. At its peak roughly 20,000 years ago, the ice sheet stretched from the Arctic Circle down to Illinois and was two miles thick in places. It shrank to its smallest size about 3,000 years ago, then started growing again about 2,000 years ago.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” Young said of the ice sheet. He noted that a piece of it survives today as the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in the Canadian territory of Nunavut, and that this remnant is still about the size of Delaware. Because the ice cap is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it, it doesn’t slide, so it preserves the vegetation underneath instead of scraping it away. When the ice expands, it entombs the plants it covers. When it recedes, it exposes them again, allowing the team to sample the moss and date it using radiocarbon dating.

“If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants,” Young said. “You’re actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin.”

That timeline is critical, according to Joerg Schaefer, also a Columbia climate geochemist. “We have a decent understanding of how this enormous ice sheet grew and disappeared over thousands of years from proxy records, but catching the start of this process with direct observations is new,” Schaefer said. “Our approach helped us see the first steps of ice-sheet growth preserved in the landscape. It gave us a rare opportunity to understand how re-glaciation begins and how the Laurentide Ice Sheet reforms.”

Technically, Earth has been in the Late Cenozoic Ice Age for about 34 million years, the researchers said. Within that span, the planet swings between glacial periods and warmer interglacial periods, and conventionally we have been in an interglacial since the last glacial period ended roughly 11,700 years ago. The new research challenges that framework by arguing that the first renewed growth of an ice sheet equals the start of a glacial period, “marking the onset of the next glaciation.” That period didn’t last long, however. The ice cap reached its maximum extent around 1960, when summer warming caused a “negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation.”

In other words, Earth’s climate had warmed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap lost more ice in the summer of 1960 than it gained the previous winter, effectively ending the next glaciation. “The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate,” the authors wrote.

The team expects the ice cap to vanish within a few centuries. Without that icy foundation, it will be harder for new ice to build up. As a result, scientists can’t say when (or where) the next glaciation might occur, especially while greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere remain high.

Young described what the ice cap’s loss will mean: “That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good,” he said. “What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6295. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?
