#6272. What Will Politics Look Like on Other Planets? It's Likely to Be a Mishmash

When we make our home on other worlds, who will be in charge?

Will it be an emperor, like the main character in âDune: Part Three,â the final movie in a trilogy based on Frank Herbertâs sci-fi saga? Or a billionaire, like the space mogul who plays a key role in setting up a Mars base in âFor All Mankindâ? Or a rebel alliance, like the revolutionaries in âStar Warsâ and âThe Moon Is a Harsh Mistressâ?

Jacob Haqq Misra, an astrobiologist who literally wrote the book on space sovereignty, suggests that itâll be none of the above, at least during the initial phases of extraterrestrial expansion.

âYouâre going to have Earth cultures represented, and ideas about Earth governance represented, and what will emerge is sort of a mishmash legal framework of agreements for how to coexist peacefully,â he says in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast. âThatâs maybe not even so bad.â

During our podcast chat, Misra laid out what sounds like a sensible perspective on the future of space politics, based on earthly precedents rather than starry-eyed assumptions about the final frontier.

For more than a decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk has talked up the prospect of building a city on Mars â and more recently, a base on the moon. But who would be in charge? Thatâs an open question even for Musk, who joked at a 2016 tech conference about being declared âking of Mars.â In a more serious vein, he said the future form of Martian government was likely to be âa direct democracy, not representative.â

âIt would be people voting directly on issues,â Musk said. âAnd I think thatâs probably better because the potential for corruption is substantially diminished in a direct vs. a representative democracy.â

Musk also had some novel ideas about the legislative process.

âIt should probably be easier to remove a law than create one,â he said. âI think thatâs probably good because laws have infinite life unless theyâre taken away. So, I think my recommendation would be something like, letâs say, 60% of people need to vote in a law, but at any point greater than 40% of people can remove it. And any law should come with a built-in sunset provision. If itâs not good enough to be voted back in, maybe it shouldnât be there.â

Misra, who is the chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space, explains in detail why it wouldnât be that easy to create a Martian government in a book titled âSovereign Mars.â The reason has to do with the Outer Space Treaty, a nearly 60-year-old agreement signed by more than 110 nations, including the United States, China, Russia and all the other space powers.

The treaty declares that all nations have the right to use the moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes, but also says no nation can claim sovereignty or ownership of extraterrestrial territory. Moreover, governments bear responsibility and legal liability for their national space activities, whether carried out by public agencies or private ventures. Which means the treaty would keep Elon Musk from being the king of Mars, even if SpaceX builds its own city.

At least thatâs the way Misra sees it. Robert Zubrin, the president of the nonprofit Mars Society, sees it differently. In his view, the treatyâs provisions mean the signatories âhave explicitly signed away their rights to interfere with Mars settlement.â But how long would it take for a Mars settlement to stand on its own, without governmental assistance?

âThere are a lot of challenges to living on Mars that make it more difficult,â Misra says. âAnd thatâs what I think is valuable about thinking about governance on Mars: not that itâs a place to start over, but itâs a way to challenge our ideas to the extreme. Maybe we never live on Mars full time, but we challenge our ideas and apply those back here on Earth.â

Misra sees plenty of earthly parallels to the sorts of issues raised by the prospect of space settlement, and they get the full treatment in âSovereign Mars.â

The author of âSovereign Marsâ is Jacob Haqq Misra, chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space. (Book cover design by Karl Janssen; Mars photo via NASA / JPL-Caltech / ASU / MSSS; author photo courtesy of Jacob Haqq Misra)

For example, consider the Antarctic Treaty System, which was set up nearly 70 years ago. The 58-nation treaty puts a freeze (heh, heh) on territorial claims of sovereignty. Administrative decisions about international activities in Antarctica are made by a 29-nation grouping of consultative parties, assisted by a secretariat based in Argentina.

Will Antarctica become independent? Misra doesnât think so â and he thinks the same line of reasoning would apply to Mars, at least in the early days of Red Planet exploration and settlement.

âTo imagine a city of a million people on Mars â Iâm not saying it wonât happen, but itâs very difficult to do so,â Misra says. âWe donât have cities that big on Antarctica. There doesnât really seem to be an economically compelling reason for it, although thereâs a lot of science on Antarctica. â¦ So, the lesson from reality and from science fiction is: Donât forget that itâs really, really hard to live in these harsh places.â

The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea serves as another instructive example. That treaty lays out principles for coordinating activities in the worldâs oceans â including the establishment of exclusive economic zones that extend 200 nautical miles beyond a nationâs territorial waters. Within those zones, each nation holds sovereign rights to resource extraction, energy production and research while still allowing for free navigation and overflight.

Even though the United States never ratified the Law of the Sea Treaty, it follows many of the treatyâs provisions due to pragmatic considerations. Misra thinks a similar sense of pragmatism will guide the settlement process on the moon and Mars.

For example, if the United States and China both establish bases at the moonâs south pole, they could agree to establish exclusive economic zones surrounding those settlements.

âI donât expect territorial conflict,â Misra says. âThe moon is really big. Itâs going to be a while before we run into the problem of two entities wanting to occupy the same place. I donât know of any regions of the moon that are so desirable that only one actor, one space agency, could get there to the exclusion of others.â

But Misra doesnât think thereâll be a new treaty to formalize a space governance system, or a new international authority along the lines of the United Earth Space Probe Agency in the fictional âStar Trekâ universe. The United Nations tried unsuccessfully to go down that road in 1979 with an international pact known as the Moon Treaty.

âItâs on the books,â Misra says. âIt has a number of signatories, but a very small number of signatories, none of which actually have their own independent launch capabilities. And so, many legal scholars consider it a dead treaty.â

Instead, Misra suspects that the worldâs space powers will find ways to âcooperate in space in a way that preserves their joint sovereignty.â

âI think there will be new multi-actor consortiums that have relevance,â he says. âThey might be outside the jurisdiction of the United Nations, for example, but they might be great things that arenât just driving forward profits for private entities. They might really reflect cooperation for science and exploration.â

What might that look like on the moon and Mars?

âProbably what would be likely is something similar to maybe a hybrid of Antarctic settlements and the way the International Space Station works,â Misra says. âIn Antarctica, there are various distances between the different outposts. Some might be closer than others, and each countryâs laws apply to that module,â he says.

The arrangements on the International Space Station are even more complicated, because each module hooked up to the outpost is the property of the nation that built the module. âYou get these weird agreements where, when data is transmitted from one section to the other, itâs actually governed by several different nationsâ laws along the way,â Misra says. âAnd if you are a Russian and you move down a couple of modules, youâre now a Russian visiting America.â

Thatâs likely to lead to a Martian mishmash. âI think you have to accept some degree of pluralism with what comes on Mars,â Misra says.

But does that mean space settlements will always be a mishmash? Not necessarily. There could be several ways to get around the Outer Space Treatyâs barriers to sovereignty. For example, an ambitious spacefaring nation could simply withdraw from the treaty, and then assert full sovereignty over the territory it controls. In 2011, space billionaire Robert Bigelow warned that China might do exactly that.

Another option would be for a company like SpaceX to move its base of operations (including its launch facilities) from the U.S. to a country that isnât a party to the Outer Space Treaty.

In âSovereign Mars,â Misra suggests a different route to extraterrestrial independence. The U.S. government, for example, could pass a law surrendering its territorial claim to an area under its control on the moon or Mars.

âIf you get the blessing from Congress, then youâve got the backing of a nation-state that says we agree with this long-term vision of establishing autonomy,â he says. âThere might be a discussion about it at the U.N., but you know, if I had to guess, if the United States did that, weâd hear about China doing something similar in a few years.â

When it comes to determining the long-term future of Martian governance, Misra actually agrees with Musk.

âWhat I think is, the Martians should decide,â Misra says. âIâm interested to see what they would think works, because it might be different models than what we come up with on Earth, simply because living on Mars is different than living anywhere here.â

More from Jacob Haqq Misra on space sovereignty:

In addition to his work as an astrobiologist and an expert on space sovereignty, Jacob Haqq Misra delves into the mysteries surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena, or UAP. He is a member of the UAP Science Advisory Council and the lead author of a study suggesting that a group of six small objects seen in a video recorded from a military aircraft near Kuwait was a flock of birds. Misra is also on the editorial review board for Limina â The Journal of UAP Studies and one of the editors of a forthcoming book titled âThe Politics of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Science, Security and Society.â

âDune: Part Threeâ opens in U.S. theaters on Dec. 18.

#6271. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6268. Students Test Prototype Landing Pad to Make Lunar Operations Safe

When spacecraft perform vertical landing and takeoff maneuvers from the lunar surface, the results are very messy! Beyond the intense heat produced by the rocket engines, the force also kicks up regolith, the particulate dust that covers most of the lunar surface. With so many crewed and cargo missions planned for the coming years, space agencies are contracting with commercial partners to develop infrastructure that will keep spacecraft, astronauts, and other surface elements safe from all "moondust."

This includes landing pads that provide a stable surface and barrier for vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) vehicles. To help them realize their objectives under the Artemis Program, NASA has enlisted engineers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) to create some. Their work is part of a multi-year partnership with Linc Research Inc., a certified engineering company located in Huntsville, Alabama, and supported through NASA's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.

The student research team is led by Dr. Judy Schneider, a professor in UAH's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Their research is focused on developing a design for modular, vented landing pads that will allow for safe transits to and from the lunar surface. This summer, the team successfully conducted three rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype of their landing pad at the university's Propulsion Research Center, demonstrating its ability to capture and redirect rocket exhaust through an integrated vent system.

Rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype lunar landing pad at the UAH Propulsion Research Center. Credit: Cadis Ammons

On Earth, landing pads consist of a solid structure capable of withstanding the full force and heat of a rocket plume. This can result in significant damage to the pad itself, as demonstrated by the first launch attempt of SpaceX's Starship prototype, including cratering beneath the mounting structure and sending debris flying in all directions. In contrast, the UAH team's design uses interlocking components with channels that help reduce thermal damage and protect the structure as well as the spacecraft.

For the tests, the team created individual concrete components and arranged them into a prototype measuring 3.65 m (12 ft) in diameter. The concrete serves as an analog for building materials that could be produced from lunar regolith, either "sintered" to form 3D-printed ceramics or combined with a bonding agent to produce "lunacrete." The components also had integrated sensors to record how the rocket plume's exhaust was channeled through the vent systems during the three firings.

The modular design also makes it easier to build on the Moon, where manufacturing centers are likely to be space-constrained. Smaller, individual components also mean future landing pads will be easier to assemble, expand, maintain, and repair over time. Combined with the use of local resources for building materials - aka. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) - the team's goal could help make large-scale lunar infrastructure more feasible.

Earth's fluffy, dense atmosphere also helps prevent rocket exhaust plumes from expanding freely and kicking up dust. Because its only natural satellite is an airless body, dust clouds caused by impacts or rockets can travel all the way to the other side of the Moon. As a result, powerful blasts during takeoff and landing can propel dust at high speeds, potentially damaging nearby habitats, power elements, equipment, and other infrastructure. The dust can also be thrown into orbit, where it could interfere with orbiting satellites, space stations, and incoming spacecraft.

This marks a major step in developing landing infrastructure that will enable a lunar base and crewed operations in the near future. As Schneider said in a UHA press release:

On Earth, we use water-cooled flame buckets to redirect rocket exhaust. But we won't have those resources on the lunar surface, where water will be in limited supply. Our goal is to redirect the rocket plume so it doesn't damage the landing vehicle or any surrounding structures. The hot-fire tests demonstrated that we could redirect the rocket plume. By using an internally vented structure, we were able to prevent the heat from damaging the pad as it could in a solid structure.

With the initial tests complete, the team is now working on a 6 m-diameter (20 ft) landing pad that will be delivered to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center (also in Huntsville) for additional testing and evaluation. These tests will further assess the design, push its technological readiness, and determine if the vented, modular approach can be scaled and adapted for repeated use. These efforts will bring the technology another step towards realization and deployment on the Moon.

Further Reading: University of Alabama Huntsville

#6267. Weather Guard’s Pack Rat Turned My Nephew's Pickup Into a Rolling Workshop

Instead of digging through tool bags and loose hardware at every stop, the Pack Rat Drawer Unit kept everything organized, secure, and within easy reach—making every job site a little more efficient.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Let’s start with a bit of transparency here: When Weather Guard sent me its Pack Rat truck toolbox, I thought it was destined for my new Honda Ridgeline. Then reality set in. While the Ridgeline is a fantastic daily driver and weekend project truck, its composite bed and in-bed trunk make it a poor match for a permanently mounted contractor toolbox. That trunk alone is a vehicle highlight, so burying it beneath a steel monolith seemed almost criminal. So instead of writing a review based on specs alone, I handed the Pack Rat over to someone who actually needed it—my nephew, a newly minted electrician who spends his days hauling electrical tools, fittings, wire, and hardware from one job site to the next.

A few hours after we installed it into his pickup and began organizing his gear, it became obvious this wasn’t just another truck accessory. It fundamentally changed how he uses his truck.

Picture a broad, low steel box bolted to the pickup bed’s floor, with a single wide drawer that pulls out over the lowered tailgate. The model we tested measures 60 inches long by 49½ inches wide, and stands 9½ inches tall. At that expanse, the top of the box system essentially becomes the new carry bed of the truck, sitting just about level with the wheel wells.

That measurement is something to be mindful of if you carry a lot of taller cargo. Trucks vary in cargo bed depth, so you’ll have to subtract 9½ inches from the overall depth of your bed to know the remaining height to the top of your bed rails. The top of the bed rails on my nephew’s Chevy Silverado 1500 sits at around 21 inches, so he still has a substantial 11½ inches to carry cargo.

To that end, for the model we tested—the 369-3-04—Weather Guard rates the top for up to 2,000 pounds evenly distributed. The drawer itself has a separate 425-pound capacity. That’s a lot of weight. It should be noted that your truck’s payload limit still applies to the combined weight of the box—about 300 pounds—its contents, and any cargo on top.

The Pack Rat is less a toolbox and more like a mobile organization system. Beneath the steel top, a massive full-width drawer rides on a set of internal rollers that allow it to glide smoothly in spite of the load within. Fully loaded with cordless tools and hardware, the drawer never sagged or bounced once. To that end, we thought pushing it shut would be a chore, but the drawer rolled back in with little effort, closing with an authoritative thunk that spoke to the solid overall build quality. It’s the kind of rolling momentum that reminds you to keep your fingers clear–not because it’s flawed in any way, but because it’s built with serious heft.

Organization is where the Pack Rat really makes its mark. Four walls fixed across the drawer space are separated by 24 adjustable divider panels. This allows you to tailor the drawer layout to fit your needs instead of forcing your tools into compartments of predetermined size. My nephew dedicated one side almost entirely to his Milwaukee cordless tool collection–drills, impact drivers, oscillating tool, batteries, and chargers–while configuring the remaining space to hold electrical supplies that change from job to job. Connectors, wire nuts, fittings, fasteners, electrical tape, and specialty tools all have designated homes, making it immediately obvious when he is in low supply on any item.

Weather Guard also paid attention to the details outside the drawer. The top surface is lined with aggressive grip tape, providing secure footing when climbing into the truck bed on damp mornings or during inclement weather. It seems like a small touch until you realize you’ll be stepping on this box as a platform throughout the day.

Before installing the Pack Rat, my nephew would often toss fittings, connectors, and hand tools into half a dozen different bags and bins. Now everything lives in one place, where it stays dry as a bone. He spends less time digging through piles of tools, knows exactly where everything belongs, and can get back to work faster. For professionals whose trucks serve as rolling workshops, those small gains in efficiency translate into real money saved over the course of months and years.

The Pack Rat is unapologetically designed for tradespeople–or at least serious enthusiasts whose vehicles are dedicated to their everyday work life. It’s a substantial piece of equipment, and that comes with trade-offs. The heavy-gauge steel construction adds noticeable weight to your vehicle, which will inevitably have some impact on your vehicle’s fuel economy. Installation is more involved than dropping, say, a Tmat organizing system or cross-over box into the bed since it’s meant to stay put. Furthermore, once installed the box consumes roughly 7 to 8 inches of vertical bed space. The tradeoff, of course, is that you retain the entire footprint of the bed above it. But if you frequently haul taller gear or equipment, that’s something to consider.

For the right buyer, though, those compromises will likely fade into the background. For years, my own truck was my office, my warehouse, my livelihood—even my diner most days. So it would have been a joy—and a value add—to have the Pack Rat at that stage of my work life. At the end of the day, having every tool, fastener, and accessory protected, organized, and within arm’s reach isn’t just convenient—it’s a real productivity upgrade.

Paul Russell Smith is a former NYC ironworker turned screenwriter (Grace Point) and home renovation specialist. #6266. A Virtual Lifeless Earth Will Help Scientists Find Life on Exoplanets

In the search for life elsewhere in the galaxy, astronomers sift through exoplanet discoveries looking for ones that could be habitable. That means rocky planets with atmospheres in habitable zones. But one thing stymies these efforts. Can we examine atmospheres and differentiate between an exoplanet that's habitable and one that's actually inhabited?

That's difficult, partly because exoplanets are so far away, and also because we only have Earth to guide us. It's the only habitable and inhabited world we know of. But new research shows how we can work with those facts to try to detect inhabited worlds.

The work is "A Whole-planet Model of the Earth without Life for Terrestrial Exoplanet Studies," and it's published in The Planetary Science Journal. The lead author is Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who was a postdoctoral astronomy student at the University of Washington when conducting this work.

"As the only known habitable (and inhabited) planet in the Universe, Earth informs our search for life elsewhere," the authors write. "Future telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will soon look for life on rocky worlds around Sun-like stars, so it is critical that we understand how to distinguish habitable planets from inhabited planets."

Observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will inject new energy into the search for life. They will shift exoplanet science from identifying worlds that could be habitable, to identifying worlds with atmospheres showing signs of life. But as the researchers point out, we still don't know how to tell inhabited worlds, if there are any, from those that are merely habitable.

"Earth is currently the only known inhabited planet in the Universe, and geological evidence suggests that it was habitable with liquid-water oceans for most of its 4.54 Gyr history," the authors write. "Owing to its long-term habitability, Earth serves as the template that guides our search for biospheres elsewhere."

The researchers tackled this issue by building a sort of virtual Earth, but one without life.

"As a first step toward answering these questions, we present a coupled interior-atmosphere evolution model of the Earth without life from 50 Myr to 5 Gyr that reproduces 19 key observations of the preindustrial Earth after 4.5 Gyr within estimated measurement uncertainties," the researchers explain. Those 19 observations included atmospheric CO2 and H2O, surface temperature and albedo, ocean mass, and even factors like upper-mantle temperature and upper-mantle heat flow. These non-biological factors all shape a planet's atmosphere and have to be accounted for.

"Though exoplanet interiors themselves will likely never be directly observable, the effects of interior evolution are apparent in the composition of the atmosphere and the albedo of the surface environment, both of which HWO will observe on Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars via reflected-light spectroscopy," the authors explain.

This schematic shows some of the key processes included in the abiotic Earth model. Remotely observable quantities (surface temperature, albedo, and atmospheric H2O and CO2) are in bold. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

The researchers also produced reflected light spectra of the model Earth that covers the likely wavelength range of the HWO. They used a code to compute a "synthetic HWO reflected-light spectra (0.2â2.0 Î¼m) for the true Earth and the abiotic Earthâs atmospheric state after 4.5 Gyr," the authors write. These included line absorptions for CO2, H2O, O2, O3, and CH4.

This virtual Earth without life can serve as a benchmark to compare with detailed atmosphere observations of habitable worlds.

âThis model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,â lead author Gilbert-Janizek said. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanetâs atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.â

This schematic shows the atmospheric sources and sinks that define the new volatile cycling processes in the model. Fluxes related to CO2 are color-coded magenta, and fluxes related to H2O are color-coded teal. The schematic doesn't include ocean chemistry. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

Gilbert-Janizek didn't start from scratch. Senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy, had already built a model that included the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation. This work added the surface and the atmosphere to build a more comprehensive model.

The authors hope that this model can serve as a kind of plug-and-play model that can be adjusted to fit with any particular exoplanet being studied. They can input factors like albedo and atmospheric CO2 and test what happens. If the model then recreates the observations of the planet, it suggests that the exoplanet in question is uninhabited.

Naturally, an undertaking of this size and complexity requires some assumptions. The model initializes after Earth's magma ocean solidified, and that dictated the atmosphere's initial composition. The authors say they chose an initial set of conditions "that apply after the bulk of the mantle has solidified."

They also assumed that plate tectonics were active during all of Earth's history beginning in the middle Hadean, which is widely believed to be true and in line with evidence. There are alternative hypotheses saying that this wasn't the case. One says that plate tectonics only began when it shifted from a stagnant-lid to modern plate tectonics during the Archaean, but the researchers avoided that.

Other assumptions were made regarding atmospheric pressure, the strength of Earth's geodynamo, and even atmospheric escape of hydrogen. But these types of assumptions are a normal part of science and are explained up front.

But the virtual Earth model successfully reproduces the properties of the Pre-Industrial Earth, and that's the most important thing. It also predicts that a planet can maintain habitable conditions for a long time without requiring the presence of life. This is relevant because false positives are one of the HWO's challenges.

These are three Engineering Architecture Concepts (EACs) for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Each one features a different mirror design. EAC-1 is a 6m, segmented, off-axis telescope. EAC-2 is the same but uses a round keystone mirror and surrounding segments. EAC-3 is an 8m on-axis telescope with round segments. Not shown is the extendable, protective barrel that each design has, which will protect the mirror from micrometeorites. Image Credit: NASA Goddard/Conceptual Image Labs

âDr. Gilbert-Janizekâs work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,â Barnes said. âAfter more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earthâs core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate.â

The question "Are we alone in the Universe" can be asked in one breath but not answered in one. It has to be broken down to much smaller questions asked and answered across many generations. Even "Are we alone in the Milky Way" is far too large and encompassing a question. "Are we alone" has to be asked exoplanet by exoplanet, and that requires tools of the sort developed by Dr. Gilbert-Janizek and her colleagues.

Our first 6,000 exoplanet discoveries were bulk discoveries. But the search is becoming more targeted toward Earth-like planets, meaning tools like this one are becoming more and more necessary. The upcoming HWO, if it gets built, places this point in even finer focus.

âRealizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists,â Gilbert-Janizek said. âIâm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe.â

#6265. Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results

In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.

For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?

A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.

Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6.5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The findings were published in Diabetes Care, a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M.D., MPH, Sc.D., of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.

Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.

Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.

The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”

Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.

“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph.D., Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”

Reference: “Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study” by Donald C. Simonson, David E. Cummings, Philip R. Schauer, Ali Aminian, Bo Hu, David E. Arterburn, John M. Jakicic, Sangeeta R. Kashyap, Ashley H. Vernon, William F. Gourash, Anita P. Courcoulas, Mary Elizabeth Patti and John P. Kirwan, 20 October 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dc26-1070

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

#6263. Kids Who Learn To Swim Early May Have an Unexpected Advantage in School

Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.

When family budgets tighten, swimming lessons can be among the first expenses to go. Most swim schools operate as commercial businesses, and cost is the biggest barrier to participation. Yet the consequences of missing out may extend beyond water safety and fitness to the skills children need when they start school.

A four-year study involving nearly 7,000 survey respondents and individual testing of 177 children suggests that children who learn to swim early have developmental advantages over their peers. Participants younger than 5 could be 5 to 18 months ahead of typical milestones in literacy, numeracy, and following instructions compared with the general population of children their age. Those advantages remained when socioeconomic background was taken into account.

Robyn Jorgensen, Emeritus Professor at the University of Canberra in Australia, examines and expands on the research in her new book, Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim.

Jorgensen does not interpret the findings as evidence that children who learn to swim are innately smarter. Instead, she argues that lessons develop skills and habits children can carry into the classroom. A child counting kicks from one to ten with an instructor, for example, is practicing number sequencing and one-to-one correspondence, matching each number to a single action.

The project grew out of a conversation between Jorgensen and Laurie Lawrence, an Olympic swim coach inducted into both the Australian and U.S. Swimming Halls of Fame. Lawrence thought children who learned to swim early generally seemed more “school-ready.”

“There was no formal evidence to support this observation, but it was one that Laurie felt he and many others in the swim industry observed,” Jorgensen explains.

To investigate that “industry hunch,” Jorgensen and her colleagues used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments. These internationally recognized testing tools were normed against national census data, providing reference standards for comparing the children’s performance with that of the wider population.

The results surprised even Jorgensen, who said, “My early observations of the young learners piqued my interest while retaining some sense of skepticism about what could be achieved. I am not from a swimming background, so had no vested interest in the ‘proving’ or otherwise of Laurie’s hunch. My only interest in swimming was as a grandparent and around water safety for my children and grandchildren, and as a recreational activity.”

Beyond the literacy and numeracy findings, the research suggests that early swimming participants are more sociable and have measurable advantages in cognitive development, language skills, and emotional regulation. These findings point to potential benefits for academic success.

“It is reasonable to claim that swimming prepares children for the schooling years, particularly the early years and the transition into schooling,” Jorgensen explains.

Access to those potential benefits is sharply unequal. Jorgensen’s analysis identifies the United States and China as having the greatest inequities in access, with regular swimming lessons affordable only to very affluent families. Singapore, Australia, Brazil, and South Africa also face substantial economic and geographic barriers.

One respondent from Zimbabwe described how lessons compete with basic necessities. “So swimming is still seen in Africa in general as elite. But basically, if you are a working-level person well below average, swimming lessons will not be a priority; what will be a priority is feeding your family.”

Even reaching a pool can be difficult. In Australia, families on remote farming properties can face journeys of hundreds of kilometers to the nearest one. The study describes “a double whammy” for children from low-income and rural communities, who are both the least likely to have access to lessons and the most at risk of drowning.

With cost-of-living pressures affecting families worldwide, Jorgensen is calling for broader government support. She argues that governments have both a moral and a financial incentive to intervene, given the billions they already spend trying to close gaps in school achievement.

“What this study has shown is that even when socioeconomic backgrounds are accounted for, children who participate in quality lessons achieve better than the general population. It would make sense for the government to consider investing in providing or subsidizing early years swimming for families who would otherwise be excluded from participation in early years swimming lessons,” Jorgensen explains.

“Investing in quality swimming lessons would make a politically wise move. The cost of lessons can be quite high, but if policies were created to offer subsidies for parents or to create swim programs for disadvantaged families, there is considerable potential for adding capital to these cohorts of learners,” she explains.

Reference: “Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim: Learnings from Participation in Early Years Swimming” by Robyn Jorgensen, 18 November 2026, Routledge. DOI: 10.4324/9781003774747

#6262. Giant Impacts Help Rocky Planets Retain Their Atmospheres

Earth's formation was a messy process. It all happened about 4.5 billion years ago, in our young chaotic Solar System. Rocky planetesimals were whizzing around in the Solar System back then, and Earth formed as more of these objects collided and merged with it.

Some of these collisions were giant impacts that generated immense heat. These were common in the later stages of Earth's formation, after the protoplanetary disk had largely dissipated and atmospheric accretion was complete. Planetary scientists have wondered how young planets like Earth could've held onto their atmospheres near the end of their accretion period. The massive heat from giant impacts should've driven primordial He/H atmospheres away. But new research suggests that simple picture doesn't capture some important details, and that giant impacts could've actually helped young rocky planets retain their atmospheres.

The work is titled "Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The authors are Darius Modirrousta-Galian and Jun Korenaga. Modirrousta-Galian is a former Yale postdoc who is now at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Korenaga is a professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

This research focuses on what happens near the end of a rocky planet's accretion process, after the protoplanetary disk has largely dissipated. This is when other planetesimals had also grown large through their own accretion processes, and when they collided with a planet like Earth, they released an enormous amount of energy.

âGiant impacts are a key part of how rocky planets grow,â said co-author Korenaga. âPlanets the size of Earth or larger are expected to form through collisions between smaller planetary bodies. These collisions add mass and release enormous amounts of heat, which can drive atmospheric escape. Their effect on a planetâs atmosphere depends on how those two changes work together.â

Modirrousta-Galian and Korenaga have been working on how planetary interiors and atmospheres evolve together and have published several papers on the topic. Their previous research laid the foundation for this work.

Their work shows that increased heat near a planet's surface isn't the only result of impacts. Some of that heat is driven deep into the planet. The impact can also "increase atmospheric gravitational binding," according to the researchers.

There are two components of a giant impact: heat and mass.

This illustration shows planetesimals in a disk around a young star. Rocky planets grow by accretion of planetesimals, and as time goes on, the planetesimals become more massive. When these massive planetesimals impact young planets, they not only generate heat, they add mass. Image Credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech.

When a planetesimal smashes into a rocky planet, the heat can be divided into two separate components. Some of it is driven more deeply into the planet where it won't drive away the atmosphere. Some of it will be mantle heat that does contribute to driving the primordial atmosphere away. But the mass gained by the accretion of the planetesimal isn't divided. All of that mass gives the planet more power to hold onto its atmosphere.

"Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature," the authors explain. "Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactorâs metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth."

"Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention," the researchers explain.

This understanding can help explain the exoplanet population.

Astronomers used to think that our Solar System was an archetype of how other solar systems would look. There would be rocky planets in the inner Solar System, gas giants further out, and ice giants beyond them. But exoplanet discoveries have cast doubt on that. The most common types of detected exoplanets aren't even represented in our Solar System: super-Earths and sub-Neptunes.

Astronomers think that super-Earths and sub-Neptunes could represent two types of planets that started out as rocky cores but ended up with much different atmospheres. Super-Earths have lost their atmospheres, while sub-Neptunes have retained more of their primordial atmospheres. A sub-Neptune only needs to retain a few percent of its H/He atmosphere to have an extended puffy atmosphere that can increase its radius by a large amount.

These are artist's impressions of the super-Earth Kepler-452b (right) and the sub-Neptune Kepler-22b (left). They're very different from each other, and both types of exoplanet are abundant in exoplanet discoveries. Giant impacts could explain their abundance. Image Credit: NASA.

âWhy nature produces both types in such abundance is a fundamental puzzle in exoplanetary science,â said Modirrousta-Galian. âWe set out to find an explanation.â

This research shows that sub-Neptunes could have grown larger through more massive impacts, and those impacts not only added mass but allowed them to retain larger atmospheres. Super-Earth's weren't subjected to those same massive impacts, and so did not gain enough mass to retain their atmospheres the same way that sub-Neptunes did. They lost theirs due to stellar radiation.

This schematic shows different outcomes for rocky planets. In one scenario, massive impacts onto a rocky create a more massive planet that can retain more of its primordial atmosphere: a sub-Neptune. In the other scenario, there are no massive impacts, no increase in rocky mass, and the planet retains less of its atmosphere. Image Credit: Darius Modirrousta-Galian

"Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth," the researchers explain. "By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths."

These results appear to overturn the long-held idea that giant impacts spelled doom for planetary atmospheres, and in turn, for the prospects of habitability. Primordial H/He atmospheres themselves didnt create habitability. But some research shows that they're essential for the development of a world that is eventually habitable, through interactions with a young rocky planet's magma ocean. These interactions may have been a significant source of Earth's water and could be on other rocky worlds, too.

âThis overturns the decades-old canonical view that giant impacts almost always lead to complete atmospheric loss, demonstrating instead that these collisions can play a crucial role in the formation of sub-Neptunes,â Korenaga said.

#6260. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

J. Gallini et al. Bias-adjusted prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy among deceased National Football League players. JAMA Network Open. 2026. doi: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.40884

M. Tiemensma et al. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in the context of longstanding intimate partner violence. Acta Neuropathologica. 2024. doi: 10.1007/s00401-024-02757-3

D.S. Priemer et al. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy in the brains of military personnel. NEJM. 2022. doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2203199

J. Mez et al. Duration of American football play and chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Annals of Neurology. 2020. doi: 10.1002/ana.25611

#6259. Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology

Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82.3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43.0% for batteries using untreated lithium.

The researchers at Xidian University developed a simple liquid coating that reacts with lithium metal to form a protective barrier. Their findings, published in Science China Chemistry, suggest a possible route toward safer, more durable batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.

Lithium metal has been called the “holy grail” of energy storage because it can theoretically store nearly ten times as much charge per gram as the graphite used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Its exceptional capacity could enable lighter batteries that store more energy and potentially support longer driving ranges.

To address this problem, researchers led by Professors Siwu Li, Weiwei Wu, and Chuang Yu combined a silicon-based polymer with indium chloride. When applied to lithium, the mixture forms lithium fluoride and lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles within a flexible protective film just 12 micrometers thick (about 0.00047 inches).

“This hybrid layer acts like a smart fortress,” explains corresponding author Siwu Li. “The polymer backbone provides flexibility to absorb the mechanical stress of lithium expanding and contracting. The lithium fluoride phase blocks electrons to prevent dendrite nucleation. And the lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles act as traffic conductors, guiding lithium ions to deposit evenly rather than piling up in dangerous spikes.”

The coated lithium electrodes withstood a critical current density of 3.5 milliamperes per square centimeter, more than four times the 0.8 achieved by untreated lithium. In complete batteries containing a nickel-cobalt-manganese oxide cathode and a sulfide solid electrolyte, the protected electrodes delivered an initial capacity of 129.8 milliampere-hours per gram and retained 82.3% after 300 cycles at 0.5C.

Spectroscopy and electron microscopy confirmed the coating’s composition and revealed a dense, uniform layer without visible cracks or gaps.

The coating could help address the chemical instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes, a major challenge in solid-state battery development.

Because the protective layer forms from an applied liquid, it may be compatible with existing industrial coating equipment without requiring expensive vacuum processing. The researchers also plan to explore alternatives to indium, including tin and zinc.

Although commercial performance remains unproven, the findings offer a promising approach to making high-energy lithium metal batteries more stable and longer-lasting.

Reference: “In situ reductive construction of a silicon-based polymer/indium alloy hybrid layer for stable lithium metal anodes in sulfide solid-state batteries” by Kun Song, Qun Zhao, Xianbo Zhao, Siwu Li, Jun Liu, Haitao Chen, Weiwei Wu and Chuang Yu, 6 August 2026, Science China Chemistry. DOI: 10.1007/s11426-026-3450-y

#6258. Game Theory Helps SETI Search for Alien Civilizations

The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 Sun-like stars for signs of Intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

In a new paper, scientists outline the effort to search for signals not only in the right place, but at the right time. The paper is "A Technosignature Survey Of The Anti-Solar Point: The SETI Institute's Largest-Ever Campaign With The Allen Telescope Array," and it was presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress. The authors are Isabel Gerrard and Sofia Z. Sheikh. Gerrard is the Technosignature Researcher with Breakthrough Listen at the University of Oxford, and Sheikh is a SETI Institute Research Scientist.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope. Itâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit." - Dr. Sofia Sheikh, SETI Institute Research Scientist.

The new search effort doesn't do away with the "where" aspect of the search. Since life exists around stars, this search is still focused on stars, or rather the planets that orbit them. But it's different this time. This time it involves a point changes over time, called the antisolar point. It's the point in space-time that's directly opposite from the Sun from the perspective of an observer.

Imagine a line extending from the Sun, through an observer on Earth, and out the other side. It's not fixed in place; it's an abstract point defined by changing coordinates that shifts as the Earth orbits the Sun.

This simple static illustration shows the antisolar point. (created with AI)

This new SETI effort is also inspired by game theory. Game theory is a way of anticipating another player's moves in a game, when their moves are also based on their anticipations of your next move. The most well-known example of game theory is probably the Prisoner's Dilemma. In this case, the other player is another intelligent civilization conducting their own SETI-like effort.

What it boils down to is trying to predict when and where we can detect a purposeful transmission from another civilization and send our own, and also when and where they're doing the same.

"We borrow from game theory the concept of Schelling points to hypothesize spacetime coordinates where both we and an extraterrestrial agent might send and search for a signal," the authors write. Schelling points are also called focal points in game theory. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this Anti-Solar Point (ASP) poses a shared and salient Schelling point."

Resources are limited, and the better we or an alien civilization can use them, the greater the chances of success. If they can figure out the most effective time and place to send a radio signal, they increase their chances of success. The same is true for us. There's a synergy in it.

"A Schelling point is a default solution two agents both naturally arrive at, without communication, because of some shared cultural understanding of prominence in the given context," the authors write. "The predictability of a Schelling point relies on a common understanding of the prominent features in this context, and the mutual awareness of each otherâs knowledge."

So without any prior communication, both we and another extraterrestrial agent would identify the same place to send and receive signals: the antisolar point. The choice is based on our shared understanding of astronomical transits, or what we call the transit method in the hunt for exoplanets. It's almost certain that another civilization would also use this method because it presents itself naturally.

"It follows that if an ETA (Extraterrestrial Agent) also used the transit method in their search for life, they would detect Earth against the Sun as habitable and classify Earth as an eligible target for interstellar communication," the researchers explain.

This simple animation shows how the antisolar point moves and how an exterrestrial observer would detect Earth's transit. (AI-generated)

At the midpoint of Earth's transit in front of the Sun, from the ETA's perspective, Earth would be directly between them and the Sun. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, once each year an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this antisolar point poses a shared and salient time-coordinate Schelling point," the authors write.

The search using the Allen Telescope Array and the antisolar point is called the ATA-ASP survey. It's a multiyear effort, and its initial findings are already here. Because it's based on the ASP, the survey isn't constant, it's intermittent. As Earth orbits the Sun, the ASP keeps changing, and it takes several years to cover it.

One of the Allen Telescope Array's dishes. The ATA-ASP survey will be the ATA's largest survey effort, collecting 11 petabytes of data over four years. Image Credit: Photo taken by Isabel Gerrard and edited by Ananya Kalapatapu

"Provided that half of the ecliptic is inaccessible in a year (the portion that is daytime), the campaign requires at least two years of observing sessions to sample every possible ASP along the ecliptic," the authors explain. "Furthermore, due to the â¼ 365.25 day orbit of the Earth (inciting the leap day every 4 years), the accessible nighttime portion of the ecliptic slightly precesses in successive years, ergo total survey coverage requires staggering observations over the course of four years." For these reasons, the ATA isn't solely occupied with the ATA-ASP survey.

The first pilot results are from August August 30th, 2024 until August 25th, 2026. Obviously, ATA-ASP didn't detect any alien signals or we would've almost certainly heard about them already. But for SETI, the results mark a milestone. Searching the ASP for signals was first proposed decades ago, and now they've finally done it.

ATA-ASP detected an enormous number of radio signals, about 1.9 million in 17 hours of observations. But they were all from human sources. Those detections were still an important test of the system though.

As things stand now, the ATA-ASP campaign has gathered another 121 nights of observations since the initial pilot. Those results haven't been shared yet.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope,â said co-author Sheikh. âItâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit. The anti-solar point gives us a way to think about that problem from the perspective of a potential sender, rather than just the receiver.â

#6256. Scientists Find a Clever Way to Read Quantum Information Without Destroying It

Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and fewer components.

Like a bit in an ordinary computer, a qubit stores information using states labeled 0 and 1. A qubit can also be prepared in a superposition, a quantum combination of the two. These states belong to a physical system that researchers build and control. In the design explored here, that system is a tiny wire connected to superconducting materials.

The aim of quantum computing is to use quantum behavior to perform certain calculations more efficiently than conventional computers. That requires control: researchers must prepare qubits and change their states deliberately. Unwanted interactions with the surroundings can disrupt them, and measuring a qubit can alter it, too.

A theoretical study proposes reading one type of qubit through an electric current it produces itself. This could let researchers follow its behavior with minimal disturbance and without the extra qubits used in many existing methods.

Andreev qubits hold information in states formed between superconducting materials, which carry electric current without resistance. They are named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who described the underlying process at the boundary between normal and superconducting materials in 1964.

“In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined – formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It’s in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed,” explains José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil.

“In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained,” says Egues.

Many existing methods use a helper quantum system called an ancilla. Researchers prepare it, connect it to the qubit, transfer information to it, and measure it to preserve the original qubit as much as possible. These steps add time and equipment. “Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself,” says Egues.

The qubit would sit in a closed superconducting circuit carrying a supercurrent, an electric current that flows without resistance. The calculations predict that interference between the states in the qubit’s superposition makes part of this current oscillate. “It’s precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It’s that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal,” Egues points out.

An applied voltage usually causes this kind of oscillation, known as the AC Josephson effect. “Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It’s the very evolution of the qubit’s state that produces that oscillation,” says Egues.

A nearby superconducting quantum interference device, or SQUID, would act as the detector. These instruments are extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields. Egues explains, “We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID ‘senses’ that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”

Identifying the qubit’s state requires knowing both the balance of 0 and 1 and their relative phase, or how the two components line up.

“Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it’s possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit,” Egues explains.

Researchers could also track the qubit through repeated readings without resetting it to its initial state after each measurement.

Simulations included measurement noise and feedback from the small detection coil. They indicated that the detector’s influence could become negligible, with readout accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%, depending on the number of measurements. These values fall within standard thresholds adopted in quantum error correction schemes.

“Our method doesn’t eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits – the ancillas – employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols,” Egues notes.

The work, published in Physical Review B Letters, was led by Egues and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. SQUID detection of extremely small currents and magnetic fields is already established, and Egues says the proposal would not require future advances in materials or device fabrication.

“All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn’t yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed,” he argues.

Reference: “Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent” by Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues and Yugui Yao, 5 August 2026, Physical Review B. DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj
