Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

#6238. Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging

If you're looking for uniformity in Nature, you won't find it in the asteroid belt. Not only are asteroid compositions different because they come from different parent bodies, but their shapes are different, too. They're not massive enough to round themselves like planets do.

This is more than just another space factoid; asteroid shapes matter. It's a near-certainty, given enough time, that a dangerous asteroid will head directly for a collision with Earth, and that's something scientists are actively studying. They want to develop ways to knock an asteroid off course, if necessary. That's what NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and the ESA's follow-up Hera mission were about.

There are multiple concepts for redirecting a dangerous asteroid. One of them is a nuclear weapon. Not to obliterate an asteroid, but to bombard it with radiation by exploding the nuclear weapon in close proximity to the asteroid. This is called a stand-off X-ray mitigation scenario. The radiation pulse will change an asteroid's course, if done soon enough and done correctly.

But the outcome of the pulse needs to be predictable to work, and that's where asteroids' different shapes come into play.

"The effectiveness of deflecting Near Earth Objects (NEOs) using pulsed radiation is challenging to quantify because it hinges critically on surface topography, which is often unknown," write the authors of new research in Icarus. The research is "Efficient computation of vapor ejecta over asteroid geometries during pulsed energy deflection," and the lead author is Nathan Moore. Moore is a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories.

A simple kinetic impactor is probably the preferred choice for deflecting an asteroid. That's what the DART mission did, and it appeared to be successful. Though it only changed the velocity of its target Dimorphos by a little, it was done soon enough to create a substantial change in its position over years.

But the more pertinent issue concerns an asteroid, or perhaps a comet, that's on a collision course with Earth, but isn't discovered soon enough for an impactor to effectively change its trajectory.

"While considered an option of last resort, it has been argued that late-time interception of a near-Earth object (NEO) or comet, either for disruption or deflection, might only be possible with the higher energy concentration available from detonation of a pulsed energy device," the authors write. 'Pulsed energy device' is one way of saying nuclear weapon. In space, there's no atmospheric shock wave from a nuclear explosion, only radiation, which is released in a powerful pulse.

"Stand-off energy burstsâthose detonated far from the surfaceâhold a potential advantage compared to surface explosions in that they might permit deflection with less disruption to the original structure, allowing for more controlled steering of the asteroid and its debris," the authors write. Disrupting the original structure might make for a good action sequence in a movie, but it would multiply the hazard to Earth by creating a swarm of debris, some of which could strike our planet.

Researchers have simulated using nuclear weapons and their radiation pulses to deflect asteroids, but their irregular shapes have stymied them. These shapes are far more difficult to model, so most research has focused on spherical asteroids. Moore and his colleagues developed a new algorithm to overcome these limitations.

âOur new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,â Moore said. âWith the old models, computers just couldnât handle it.â

In this research, the authors simulated known asteroids with more irregular shapes, an important improvement on previous work.

"The approach improves on earlier methods by accounting for the actual topography of the asteroid fully in three dimensions without unacceptably increasing computational cost or reducing accuracy," the authors explain. "As a demonstration, we predict the deflection of three bodies of different shapeâasteroid (101955) Bennu, asteroid (25143) Itokawa, and asteroid (6489) Golevkaâfrom both near-field and far-field irradiations."

These images of asteroids Itokawa (left) and Bennu (middle), and a computer model of asteroid Golevka (right), show how asteroid shapes can be very different from one another. Image Credits: Itokawa: By ESO, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=170826264. Bennu: By NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona - Public Domain. Golevka: By NASA/JPL - NASA - Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Public Domain.

A sequence of events unfolds after a nuclear device is detonated near an asteroid. First, an intense x-ray pulse is directed at one side of the asteroid. Then there's rapid surface vaporization, and that creates most of the deflection thrust. Next is an internal shock wave, a powerful blow that travels through the asteroid's body. Finally, the internal structure of the asteroid is fractured, and that can blow chunks of the asteroid off the surface opposite the blast, and off of the asteroid's sides.

So despite there being no atmospheric shock wave, the asteroid is still disrupted.

The results highlighted how important an asteroid's shape is. Depending on which side of the asteroid was facing the radiation blast, the deflection velocity can be up to five times greater. "We find that the orientation of the body at time of intercept can increase the deflection velocity by up to nearly 2Ã for Bennu, 4Ã for Itokawa, and 5Ã for Golevka, compared to the minimum response for each body," the authors write.

This figure shows the pressure distribution as averaged over the first 20 Î¼s of vapor expansion, for asteroid (a) Bennu, (b) Itokawa, and (c) Golevka, for near and far Height Of Bursts (HOB). The vaporization is what creates most of the deflection thrust. Image Credit: Moore et al. 2026. Icarus.

âWe expected aim to matter,â said lead author Moore in a press release. âWhat surprised us was how much.â

The simulation in this work can be used on any asteroid that's been mapped by a spacecraft during a flyby. The size of the explosion, the distance, and the surface exposed to it can all be calculated in advance. By calculating the surface vaporization, the main factor in deflection, the simulation determines how hard the asteroid will be pushed, how fast it will rotate, and how much of the surface might break up.

The interior structure of asteroids can be quite different, and that's beyond the capabilities of this model to account for. "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We canât predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Real life is always different from simulations, and that means that these results can't tell us with absolute certainty what will happen. But it's a step forward, one that drives home how critical the aim is to a successful asteroid deflection, should one be needed in the future.

"The strong sensitivity of deflection and disruption to asteroid topography is especially pertinent given that the shape of an incoming NEO might not be known, and its orientation at time of intercept may be uncontrolled," the authors write. Their work as it stands now can at least be used to make estimates, which is better, far better, than nothing.

"Alternatively, effort could be made to obtain high-resolution topographic characterization of an incoming NEO to improve accuracy of the deflection model, such as using spacecraft-based imagery or altimetry acquired before detonation," the authors explain.

It's possible that asteroid-mapping spacecraft could stand at the ready in space, waiting to be deployed. They could even be paired with asteroid-disrupting spacecraft carrying nuclear weapons. Or the two capabilities could be combined into one spacecraft. Placing atomic weapons in space would be extremely tricky in our fractured geopolitical world, but it's still a possibility, maybe the only possibility.

But however we prepare for an incoming asteroid, this work highlights how important it is that our aim is true.

âOur study shows how important it is to aim carefully,â Moore said. âPick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.â

#6236. Popular Dairy Alternatives Could Be Leaving You Short of Essential Nutrients

Replacing even a modest amount of dairy with plant-based alternatives could significantly reduce essential nutrient intake, according to a new study from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that substituting just 20% to 35% of dairy products increased the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake among adolescent girls from 54% to 65%. Among women ages 19 to 49, the figure rose from 32% to 42%.

The study also identified reductions in calcium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12 intake. However, researchers found that fortifying plant-based alternatives and other foods could help prevent these nutritional shortfalls.

In the first UK study of its kind, researchers from the University of Surrey and Queen’s University Belfast analyzed dietary data from more than 3,500 people, ages 18 months to 100 years. Using the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, they modeled how replacing milk, yogurt, and cheese with commercially available plant-based alternatives would affect intake of four essential micronutrients.

Dr Katie Nicol, a research fellow at the University of Surrey and co-author of the study, explained:

“With the growing need to address environmental sustainability, many dietary recommendations are focused on plant-based diets and the reduced intake of animal products.”

“With the rise in plant-based alternative foods, we need to know whether they are like-for-like replacements for the micronutrients that are found in dairy products. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups, including young children and adolescent females, who are more likely to be deficient in certain micronutrients, which could affect their overall health.”

Iodine was the nutrient most affected by dairy replacement. When researchers modeled completely replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives under current fortification levels, the estimated prevalence of inadequate iodine intake reached 80% among adolescent girls and 72% among adolescent boys. These figures reflect modeled dietary inadequacy, not confirmed clinical deficiencies.

Iodine is essential for producing thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism and support growth and brain development. It is particularly important before and during pregnancy, when iodine requirements increase.

Dr Sarah Bath, associate professor at the University of Surrey and lead author, said:

“The UK is particularly vulnerable to iodine insufficiency due to a lack of an iodine fortification policy such as universal salt iodization, which many other countries have.”

“People may also be unaware of the importance of iodine, which is needed to make thyroid hormones to regulate our metabolism, support healthy growth, and brain development. Iodine is particularly important during pregnancy, when the requirement increases, but it is also essential prior to pregnancy to ensure that stores are optimized. People are also unaware that dairy products are a major source of iodine, particularly in the UK, and that plant-based alternatives, unless fortified, have a very low iodine content.”

The researchers found that mandatory fortification of plant-based dairy alternatives could prevent declines in micronutrient intake. However, even with fortified alternatives, an estimated 59% of adolescent girls would still have inadequate iodine intake. Adding iodine to bread reduced that figure to 37%, suggesting that combining both fortification strategies could be more effective.

Dr Nicol emphasized the importance of aligning nutrition policies with environmental goals:

“Nutrition policy must evolve in tandem with environmental targets; however, it is important that shifts towards more sustainable diets do not compromise on public health. Fortification of foods is one way that this could be achieved; however, government policy is needed to make this happen.”

Dr Anne Nugent, from Queen’s University Belfast, described how the team identified dairy-containing foods in the UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey and modeled replacing them with equal amounts of plant-based alternatives. The researchers accounted for differences in the nutritional content of available products and tested whether fortification could prevent deficiencies without causing excessive nutrient intake.

“During the analysis, we first identified all foods and recipes containing dairy produce (milk, cheese, and yogurt) in the national food survey for the UK, the National Diet and Nutrition Survey. Next, we conducted a series of replacement scenarios whereby we substituted the dairy present with an equal weight of plant-based dairy alternatives. As the nutrient composition of dairy alternatives available on our supermarket shelves can vary, we also applied a condition to make sure that every dairy alternative we had identified in our previous market survey had an equal chance of selection. The last step was to examine the impact on dietary intakes of key nutrients following either the reduction or removal of dairy from the diet, replacing it with the dairy alternatives as above, and asking whether a series of fortification options could mitigate against any shortfalls in intake while avoid situations of excess.”

Reference: “The impact of replacing dairy products with plant-based dairy alternatives on iodine and other micronutrients: a modelling study and evaluation of policy options to support population intake” by Katie Nicol, Anne P Nugent, Jayne V Woodside, Kathryn H Hart and Sarah C Bath, , The Lancet Planetary Health. DOI: 10.1016/j.lanplh.2026.101515

#6235. Scientists Discover Something Unexpected 90 Kilometers Beneath Earth

A rock from Papua New Guinea was hotter than expected during its descent into Earth, challenging models of a process that influences earthquakes, volcanoes, and climate.

Earth recycles its own surface. In regions called subduction zones, one tectonic plate, a vast slab of Earth’s outer shell, sinks beneath another as the plates collide. These zones are sites of earthquakes and volcanic activity, and they help stabilize Earth’s climate over millions of years by recycling molecules such as carbon dioxide.

A rock from Papua New Guinea has revealed a gap in scientists’ understanding of the temperatures inside these regions. Four million years ago, it descended more than 90 kilometers, or about 56 miles, below Earth’s surface. But roughly halfway down, it was already much hotter than current models would predict.

An international research team led by Göttingen University reconstructed the journey by studying eclogite, a red and green rock that forms under the high pressures found in subduction zones. Minerals within the rock preserve evidence of the conditions it experienced underground, allowing researchers to piece together its history. The findings were published in Nature Geoscience.

Using a combination of analytical techniques, the researchers found tiny inclusions of coesite trapped inside another mineral during the rock’s formation. Coesite is a mineral that requires extremely high pressure to form. Its presence helped the team conclude that the rock had reached a depth of at least 90 kilometers, where it experienced temperatures of around 800°C, or 1,470 °F.

At about 45 kilometers, or 28 miles, however, the rock had been only 100°C cooler, a difference of 180°F. In other words, it had already reached around 700°C, or 1,290°F, at roughly half the depth. Those shallower conditions were unusually hot, while the deeper conditions fit the more common, relatively cold pattern of subduction. Calling the deeper conditions cold does not mean the rock cooled as it sank. It means that its temperature was lower relative to its depth than it had been earlier in the journey.

Dr. Jan Schönig at Göttingen University’s Geoscience Center explains, “Finding this change from hot to cold subduction was unexpected, as this contradicts our current thermal models of subduction zones.”

Researchers have found rocks that recorded unexpectedly high temperatures before. This is the first time, though, that a rock’s journey from shallow to deep conditions has so clearly shown an accompanying shift to relatively colder temperatures for its depth.

One possible explanation is that shearing stress, produced as plates move against one another, heats rocks at shallow depths more than scientists have assumed. Another is that the subduction zone had not yet had enough time to develop the lower temperatures expected there. Both processes could have contributed.

Understanding these temperatures more accurately could help researchers assess how subduction affects earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the movement of chemicals through Earth, including the long-term carbon cycle. It could also clarify how subduction has operated over millions to billions of years and how it continues today.

Reference: “Geothermal gradient change during subduction recorded by ultrahigh-pressure eclogite” by Jan Schönig, Silvio Ferrero, Kerstin Gresky, Dominik Sorger, Axel K. Schmitt, Bernd Wunder, Suzanne L. Baldwin and Adam F. Holt, 1 October 2026, Nature Geoscience. DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02110-1

The research was supported by funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG).

#6234. 'Big Bang' Fix Puts Voyager Across the 'One Light-Day' Mark

An innovative solution helps to put the venerable Voyager 1 spacecraft past a key milestone.

Flashback to 1977. Jimmy Carter was U.S. president, Star Wars was a box office hit, and the two Voyager spacecraft departed on an historic Grand Tour of the solar system. Now, teams at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory are working to keep the missions active, as they push the boundaries of interstellar space beyond the solar system.

NASA recently announced that after a brief bit of drama and loss of communications with Voyager 1, a fix dubbed the âBig Bangâ was successful in resuscitating the spacecraft. The Big Bang swap alternated three units (two primary heaters and an old 8-track digital tape recorder) with three low power secondary options. The brief loss of communications occurred on October 20th, and lasted for 48 hours.

Engineers work on a Voyager spacecraft prior to launch. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

âThis is the first time weâve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,â said Kareem Badaruddin, in a recent press release. âWeâre relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.â

The Big Bang method was also successfully implemented to keep Voyager 2 functioning this past August.

Traveling far from the Sun, the Voyager missions rely on Plutonium-fueled radioisotope thermoelectric generators for power. PU-238 has a half-life of just under 88 years, meaning the missions are now steadily losing power.

This loss equates to about 4 watts of power each year. Voyager 1 currently utilizes a little over 200 watts of power, about enough to power an electric blanket. This has forced mission controllers to make some tough choices, including turning off the Low Energy Charged Particle experiment LECP in early 2026. The missions launched with 10 instruments in 1977.

The swaps had to occur at the same time, as the units involved also heat the spacecraft and assure that it continues to operate in the chilly depths of deep space.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, actually after Voyager 2. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. A flyby past enigmatic Titan to get a close look on November 12, 1980 meant the mission would depart the plane of the solar system afterwards. Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

The paths of Voyagers 1 and 2 out of the solar system. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

The Voyagers continue to do science as they travel through interstellar space beyond the fringes of the outer solar system. The two Voyagers are the first missions to sample the region of space beyond the heliosphere directly.

The Voyagers head out beyond the bowshock of the solar system into interstellar space. Credit: NASA

Right now, the important Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS) plus a magnetometer instrument on Voyager 1 remain active. Without the Big Bang shuffle, mission controllers would have had to make the hard decision turn off yet another crucial instrument in 2027.

Voyager 1 witnesses a 'crescent Saturn'. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Moving at 16.9 kilometers per second relative to the Sun and the solar system, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made artifact to reach the one light-day mark this month on Wednesday, November 18th at 5:16 AM EST. Thatâs roughly 26 billion kilometers or 172 Astronomical Units (AU) distant. For context, the Moon and cis-lunar space marking the farthest humans have traveled to date is just over one light-second distant.

NASAâs global Deep Space Network continues to monitor the ever fainter signals from the Voyager spacecraft. Controllers will likely have to contend with more signal outages in the years to come.

The worldwide DSN tracks missions including one of the Voyager spacecraft. Credit: NASA/DSN

Along with the now silent Pioneers 10 and 11 and the still active New Horizons mission, Voyagers 1 and 2 are now leaving the solar system for galactic space. The upper stage Star boosters that help these missions achieve escape velocity are on their way outbound as well. The next mission escaping the solar system wonât happen for a while, though the proposed Interstellar Probe mission could one day make the trip. Voyager 1 is now outbound in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus near its border with Hercules.

Congrats the intrepid and resourceful Voyager 1 team. Hopefully the mission will surpass its half-a-century birthday in space, coming right up next year.

#6233. The 7 Best Electric Chainsaws of 2026

Cordless battery-powered chainsaws are quiet, light, and fast—everything you need for a spring refresh.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal. Electric chainsaws have come a long way and, in most cases, closed the gap to their gas-powered cousins—they’re easy to start (just push a button or two in most cases), generate little noise, produce no fumes, and simplify maintenance. We’ve tested electric saws as big as 20 inches and they’re powerful enough to bring down a mature tree.

Saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners. For cleaning up after storms, felling small to medium-size trees, and regular pruning or arboreal maintenance, an electric chainsaw is the ideal choice.

We noted how well each chainsaw endured prolonged use. Making repeated cuts can cause a chainsaw, and its battery, to heat up. If it gets too hot, it will trigger a thermal limit and the saw’s overload protection will shut it down. We also considered comfort, vibration, saw balance, and ease of use to make our final recommendations.

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops our list of chainsaws for two main reasons: run-time and constant, consistent power. These are the two most common concerns or complaints we hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw tested. But that’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Aside from run-time and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. Note that Stihl positions the MSA 260 C-O “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost, $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So, if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Husqvarna may not have been the fastest-cutting electric chainsaw we tested, but it’s at the top of our list because it does just about everything well—it operates smoothly, cuts fast (enough), and is easy to use. With the boost button engaged, it blazed through our cutting tests, slicing through an 8-inch log in about 5 seconds. It also had the fastest windup speed of any electric chainsaw that I personally tested—it was ready to cut as soon as I pulled the trigger. Even with its impressive power, this chainsaw is surprisingly quiet, producing 67 decibels at 60 feet. The Power Axe isn’t particularly light at 14.5 pounds with battery, but it’s well balanced. I had no problem holding it steady even when making cuts at waist-level height.

The Power Axe also comes with a suite of well-designed, user-friendly features. The power button and boost button are located just above the handle so they’re easier to access on the fly. You also have the ability to adjust the chain tension by hand, loosening a dial to release the tension, then rotating a dial to tighten it back up. The whole process takes seconds. There’s also a built-in chain brake to protect from injuries. It’s a well-built, high-performing electric chainsaw that still manages to come in at a reasonable price.

Echo’s DCS-5000 gives you what you want most out of a chainsaw: raw cutting power. It may lack some of the bells and whistles you’ll find on pricier models, such as tool-less chain tensioning and power-saving settings, but its base performance is right up there with the Power Axe 350i. The DCS-5000 cut through 8-inch hardwood in less than 4 seconds. That's saying something considering that the DCS-5000 costs at least $100 less than any other saw that can do the same.

Along with its impressive cutting speed, the Echo is also relatively light at just over 12 pounds. I could feel the difference whenever I had to lift it up above shoulder-height to cut higher limbs, or while crouching down to cut a fallen 8-inch beech tree.

There is a trade-off with the DCS-5000, though, in that it lacks any kind of quality-of-life-related features. You won’t find tool-less chain tensioning or ECO settings that conserve battery life here. It’s pretty loud, too, producing 76 decibels at 60 feet. And, finally, while I appreciated the lighter weight, I could also feel the vibrations in my arm more than electric chainsaws with more refined builds.

Still, if you don't mind the rougher feel, higher noise level, and lack of a few user-friendly features you’ll find on pricier electric chainsaws, the Echo DCS-5000 offers exceptional value.

The newest saw from Makita, the 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw, is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50-cc gas saw, and we’re inclined to agree. The first pull of the trigger surprised us with the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

Using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees, or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as big as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering. The 40V Max XGT chainsaw, at 20-inches, is among the biggest battery powered chainsaws we test. Our test unit came as a kit, with everything you need, including an 8.0Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

The Stihl MSA 80 is an easy-to-use chainsaw that also packs impressive cutting power. Its compact build—the 14-inch saw weighs about 10 pounds—gives it a balanced feel in hand. It features a narrow bar that makes it easier to fit it into the crotches of trees for pruning than other electric chainsaws we tested like the Ego 20-inch chainsaw or Husqvarna Power Axe 350i. Likewise, it comes equipped with a thinner chain that cuts more smoothly through wood, producing less vibration. Lastly, its variable speed trigger allows you to adjust the speed of the blade to suit the job at hand.

There are several user-friendly features worth noting. Chain adjustments are effortless: Simply loosen a knob, turn the adjuster, and tighten the knob. There’s also a lubrication system to keep the chain moving with a minimal amount of bar oil.

Stihl’s chainsaws come at a premium price, and this one is no different. At $500, the MSA 80 is the most expensive electric chainsaw we tested, despite having a relatively short bar. Even so, it’s an ideal choice for homeowners who are looking for professional-grade build quality and performance out of an electric chainsaw.

If you already have other Echo tools, like a leaf blower or trimmer, then you can save a little cash and purchase the DCS-2500T as a tool only.

There’s a price for the CS-2005’s cutting power and capacity, though—its weight. While we liked its buttery smooth operation, it weighs an arm-burning 19.3 pounds with a battery. Making cuts on limbs above the head or below the knees was a far more challenging experience than with electric chainsaws we tested that were 4 to 5 pounds lighter. The Ego CS-2005 also lacks a tool-free chain tensioning system. If you don’t mind the extra heft, the Ego CS-2005 is the high-powered electric you’ll want for really big jobs.

As new models come out, we can’t keep all the models we test on our recommended list. But some of these older models and runners-up are still worth considering. Here are a few:

Milwaukee M18 Fuel 18V 16-Inch Electric Chainsaw: Don’t be fooled by the Milwaukee’s lower voltage, this saw has plenty of power for quickly cutting up large limbs or felling medium-sized trees. It’s a good saw, but we’d mostly recommend it to folks already on Milwaukee’s M18 platform, so you can buy it as a tool only and save some money.

Stihl GTA 26: While folks often refer to tools like this as “mini chain saws”, Stihl bills the GTA 26 as a garden pruner. Intended specifically for pruning shrubs and small branches, the GTA 26 combines light weight and a pistol-like configuration to make an easy-to-handle tool. Think of it as a power loppers, with greater size capability.

Worx Nitro WG385 40V 16-Inch Chainsaw: At less than $300, the Worx Nitro WG385 can get the job done. It’s lighter and easier to maneuver than other similarly sized saws, but it’s also a little less powerful, with a little less run-time. Still, with some patience we were able to find it useful for basic property maintenance. For the price, the Worx Nitro WG385 is a good cost-effective option for occasional use.

At the heart of an electric chainsaw is its motor and battery, which need to work in concert to perform well. The longer the chainsaw bar, the bigger the log or tree you can cut. So, the motor has to have enough torque and speed, while the battery has to be able to deliver the power needed to sustain that torque and speed. This is one reason why bigger saws can cost a lot more than smaller ones. Batteries are a significant factor in the price of a saw, and bigger batteries cost more. Battery size is typically measured in amp-hours (Ah), and larger saws will typically have 8 to 12 Ah batteries.

Mini chainsaws, made for pruning and other small jobs, feature a one-handed design with a small cutting bar—4 to 8 inches—and a small battery. If you need to break down large branches from trees, opt for a smaller full-size chainsaw with a 12- to 14-inch cutting bar. For something professional-grade, consider a large chainsaw with a 16- to 20-inch cutting bar and larger battery.

Among electric chainsaws with comparable bar lengths, those with larger batteries will typically have more ripping power, which means they’ll cut through limbs and logs more quickly, allowing you to get the job done faster. Just keep in mind that a more powerful chainsaw is also often a heavier chainsaw.

An electric chainsaw’s runtime depends on the capacity of its battery, in amp-hours. Broadly speaking, more capacity means more juice, but larger saws draw more power per second, so it’s not uncommon to find large chainsaws with large batteries getting comparable battery life to their smaller, more efficient counterparts.

Since your chainsaw only uses power when you’re using it to cut, its true runtime comes down to how many cuts it can make on a single charge. The Popular Mechanics test team tests runtime by checking how many times each model cuts through a 6-inch log on a single charge. Depending on battery size and chainsaw power, that number can vary quite a bit—from as low as 50 to as high as 300.

The “cutting bar” is the business end of the chainsaw—the long, rounded metal guide that the chain spins around to create a blade. The length of the bar, which is measured from the base of the chainsaw’s head to the tip of the cutting bar, determines the maximum thickness of the wood that your chainsaw can cut through in a single pass. Generally speaking, your chainsaw can safely cut through limbs with a diameter up to 2 inches less than the length of the bar. For example, a 12-inch chainsaw can cut through a limb up to 10 inches in diameter in a single pass.

For a long time, going electric meant settling for a chainsaw with a shorter bar, but that’s no longer the case. While gas engines offer more power, especially in larger saws, there are electric options with professional-length cutting bars. For instance, a 20-inch electric chainsaw has the power to bring down mature trees.

Need is an important distinction here. We don’t recommend picking the most powerful saw with the longest cutting bar within your budget. A longer bar will give you more cutting capacity, but it’s also heavier and more difficult to handle safely. We recommend buying the tool that’s just big enough for the cutting tasks you’ll perform regularly. If you’re looking to trim small limbs and branches, a pruning saw with a 4- to 8-inch bar such as the Stihl GTA 26 is going to be the best choice. If you’re taking down trees and breaking them down for firewood, you may need something longer.

It’s important that you feel comfortable handling the weight of your chainsaw. If it’s too heavy to hold at chest height, then you can’t use it safely.

With electric chainsaws, weight is directly related to the length of the cutting bar. The longer the cutting bar, the heavier the chainsaw. A mini chainsaw with an 8-inch bar will weigh around 5 pounds, while a large 18-inch chainsaw can weigh as much as 15 pounds.

One thing to keep in mind: Many manufacturers list the “bare” weight of their cordless chainsaws without the battery, so when you do add that in, it can mean an extra 1 to 3 pounds to the load.

Chainsaws are among the most dangerous power tools you can put your hands on: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), some 36,000 people ends up in the hospital with chainsaw-related injuries each year.

That is why it’s crucial to always take every step you can to ensure the safest possible conditions when using a chainsaw. A good electric chainsaw should have built-in safety features to minimize the possibility of an accident: First, look for a trigger lock, which requires you to maintain pressure on a button near the handle to keep the chain spinning. Most will also have a chain brake at the front of the handle, which disengages the chain if the chainsaw kicks back.

That depends on the size of the tree. Even the largest electric chainsaws with a 20-inch cutting bar only have the torque necessary to cut down moderately tall trees. You’ll want a gas chainsaw that brings the extra power to bring down an older, larger tree, or if you’re bringing trees down regularly.

Electric chainsaws don’t require much maintenance. Use a brush or cloth to remove sawdust and other debris that’s caught in the chain and sprocket area after each use.

You should also clean any debris that’s fallen into the air intake slots: Brush it away material on the outside with a clean paintbrush, then blow the valves out with compressed air.

Lastly, electric chainsaws have an auto-lubrication mechanism, but we recommend checking the chain oil reservoir before each use, and refilling it if necessary.

Many cordless electric chainsaws are water resistant and will work fine in the rain. Before you take one for a spin, check its Ingress Protection rating (IP), which measures dust and waterproofing. If your chainsaw features an “IPX3” rating, it can handle “sprays of water” and should be fine in light rain. An “IPX4” rating can withstand moderate to heavy rain.

All that said, we don’t really recommend operating a chainsaw in the rain. Even with work gloves, rain makes every chainsaw-related job less safe, so hold off until the sun comes out if you can.

You should never use a corded electric chainsaw in the rain. Doing so presents a significant electrocution risk. (It’s one of many reasons we generally don’t recommend them.)

#6232. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6231. Earth's Gravity May Have Kept the Early Moon's Volcanic Heart Beating

We typically think of the Moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics - the Moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But, some lunar material returned from the Changâe-5 mission was notably formed only around two billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin. So how did a world that was supposed to have settled down without volcanism remain hot enough to create these materials more than two billion years after its violent birth? A new paper from Miao Chen of the Chengdu University of Technology and his colleagues, and recently published in the journal Planet, offers an explanation - tidal heating.

Letâs first set the stage of the Moonâs creation. Our best guess is that it was created when another early protoplanet, named Theia, slammed into Earth in a massive collision, creating a chunk of debris that coalesced into the Moon. However, that amount of debris was relatively small - only about a quarter the size of the Earth itself, which meant the internal heat generated during its formation would rapidly radiate away, turning the Moon itself geologically dormant.

But when Changâe-5 returned some lunar basalts from Oceanus Procellarum back to Earth, laboratory dating showed them to be only around two billion years old. Basalts are only formed in active volcanoes, or other environments with similarly high pressures and temperatures. Environments that, at least according to traditional geological theory, shouldnât have existed on the Moon two billion years ago.

Fraser explains why the Moon is moving farther away.

Despite that, scientists have tried offering other solutions. Radioactive elements, such as potassium and uranium, emit some heat as they decay. But there wasnât enough un-decayed material left on the Moon to offer the amount of heat needed to form basalt two billion years ago. Asteroid strikes could cause localized high impact thermal spikes, but the heavy bombardment period that gave the Moon most of its craters had ended long before the basalt was formed.

So instead the authors turned to gravity - specifically to a phenomenon called tidal heating. This happens when a celestial body is squeezed, stretched, and kneaded as it travels in an elliptical orbit around a larger parent body. Perhaps the most famous example of this in the solar system is Io. This moon of Jupiter is constantly erupting due to the tidal squishing it undergoes during its orbit around the largest planet.

Obviously, the Moon doesnât seem to be undergoing any such squishing currently. However, two billion years ago, the Moon was much closer to the Earth than it is today, orbiting our planet in sixteen days rather than the twenty seven it takes now. Its orbit was also much more eccentric, looking much more like an oval than a circle. All of which means that Earth itself exerted huge rhythmic tidal forces on the Moon' s interior during the course of its orbit.

Fraser details Tidal Locking, which also affects the Moons geology.

Weâve known that for awhile, but astronomers have always modeled the Moon as a mostly uniform sphere when trying to understand how these gravitational squeezes affected it. However, scientists knew this was a simplification - there is an ultra-low viscosity zone of rock wrapping itself between the Moonâs core and mantle. When the research team plugged a more realistic 3D representation of the mantle setup into a convection simulation, they noticed that a ton of energy was directed specifically at two symmetric regions along the lunar core-mantle boundary.

These regions, which they named Tidal Heating Anomaly Zones (THAZs) , absorbed a huge amount of energy. They calculated that, around 3.2 billion years ago, despite taking up only 2.5% of the mantleâs total volume, the tidal strain on these regions delivered 150 gigawatts of power - more than four times the amount of energy generated by radioactive decay.

This seemed to be the driving force behind much of the Moonâs geological history. It helped keep the lunar core warm, which helped sustain a magnetic field for much longer the models originally predicted (and was a puzzle when scientists realized that Apollo lunar samples seemed to have formed in a strong magnetic field). It also drove huge mantle plumes that swelled toward the crust. Billions of years later, long after the tidal engine has calmed down, those stranded pockets of mantle melted to produce the basalts seen in the Changâe-5 samples.

If thereâs one thing thatâs clear from the paperâs theory, it's that we still donât know a lot about the Moonâs geological history. This new model offers some elegant answers to some of the most persistent questions in that area, but as of now itâs still only a theory. Maybe some of the numerous lunar missions planned over the next decade will be able to provide more definitive data to finally solve the evolutionary questions of our nearest neighbor.

#6230. Scientists Finally Crack a 1,600-Year-Old Roman Glass Mystery

More than 1,600 years after the Romans created the famous Lycurgus Cup, a University of Sheffield technician has found a way to reliably reproduce its extraordinary color-changing glass.

A glass cup made more than 1,600 years ago has puzzled historians and glassmakers for centuries.

When light reflects off its surface, the cup appears jade green. When light shines through it, the glass turns a striking ruby red. Despite knowing much about the science behind this unusual effect, modern glassmakers have struggled to reproduce it consistently. Now, researchers at the University of Sheffield have developed a recipe that recreates the remarkable color-changing properties of this ancient Roman masterpiece.

The Lycurgus Cup, created in the fourth century AD and housed in the British Museum, is made from a special type of glass known as dichroic glass. Its appearance changes depending on whether light reflects from the surface or passes through the material. The cup is one of only 40 surviving Roman glass cage cups and among the most complete. It is also the only surviving example known to display this extraordinary color-changing effect.

Its craftsmanship is just as remarkable as its colors. The decoration depicts Lycurgus, a mythical Thracian king, entangled in vines as punishment for his misdeeds. In 2022, an international panel of artists and conservators recognized the cup as one of the seven glass wonders of the world, honoring its artistry, unusual colors, and exceptional preservation.

Scientists believe the secret lies in tiny amounts of gold and silver added to the glass by Roman craftspeople. Under the right conditions, these metals can form layered nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because the particles are smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, they absorb light strongly and produce vibrant colors that depend on their size and shape.

Understanding this process, however, is different from knowing exactly how to recreate it. The precise techniques used by Roman glassmakers remain unknown, and previous attempts to reproduce the effect have met with varying degrees of success.

The challenge took on new life when Christina Metcalfe, project manager for the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project, asked University of Sheffield technician Dr. Lisa Hollands to recreate the glass for the university’s LightFest in 2025.

“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” said Dr. Hollands, from the University’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.

“I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.

“To start with, I worked with a leading Roman glass expert, Professor Caroline Jackson, to research what was already known about glass of the time and developed a base glass using modern materials to mimic what the Romans might have used. Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form.

“Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”

Hollands experimented with different types of furnaces, starting materials, and oxygen levels, even testing the addition of sugar. After numerous attempts, she developed a glass that appeared opaque green under reflected light but turned red when illuminated from behind. The successful sample demonstrated that the distinctive optical effect of the ancient cup could be recreated using modern materials and experimental techniques, although it did not establish the exact recipe used by the Romans.

The first piece was exhibited at LightFest, an event held in Sheffield by the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project in partnership with the Universities of Sheffield and Bristol. Funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), the project focuses on developing materials that harness light for sustainable technologies. These materials could support fields important to the United Kingdom’s economy, including solar energy, quantum technologies, and healthcare diagnostics.

With the glass recipe established, the team wanted to create something that would showcase its unusual properties while paying tribute to the original Roman artifact.

“The next step was to commission a piece worthy of paying homage to its illustrious predecessor.

“We approached Elliot Walker, one of the UK’s finest glass artists and winner of season two of Netflix’s Blown Away, who accepted the challenge and was commissioned to create a contemporary sculpture using Dr Hollands’ recipe,” said Metcalfe.

For Walker, working with a material inspired by ancient glassmaking offered a rare connection to the craftspeople who had mastered similar techniques centuries earlier.

“It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one.

“You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands.”

Walker drew inspiration from both the story depicted on the Lycurgus Cup and the classical Farnese Atlas sculpture. His design also needed to make the unusual optical effect visible to viewers, which influenced the final form of the artwork.

“I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass,” Walker explained.

“The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup.”

The completed sculpture is scheduled to be unveiled at the Millennium Gallery during the University of Sheffield’s Festival of the Mind, running from November 6 to 15, 2026. After the festival, it will become a permanent exhibit at the Turner Museum of Glass, located within the university’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.

“We set out to create something tangible to help the public understand what is possible when these tiny nanoparticles are embedded in something,” Metcalfe said.

“What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations. The incredible historic narrative really captures people’s imaginations, and I like to think we’ve created something that people will marvel at for years to come.”

Although this particular glass is expected to have mainly decorative uses, the knowledge gained from recreating it could contribute to the development of new photonic materials and advanced glasses for managing radioactive waste.

The project also connects with ongoing research led by Professor Russell Hand at the university’s Immobilisation Science Laboratory (ISL), within the School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering. His work focuses on immobilizing complex nuclear wastes in glass, a process intended to keep hazardous materials safely contained.

Magma and a possible environment for ancient life might be present on Mars in the region of a large volcano on the Red Planet.

A noxious gas found seeping through cracks on Mars hints that there may be magma flowing beneath the Red Planet's surface — and perhaps even an environment similar to habitable ones on Earth, a new study suggests.

Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) spacecraft spotted a possible signal of hydrogen chloride gas leaking from rifts in the region of Alba Mons, the largest volcano on Mars in terms of surface area. (Mars' famous Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in terms of height.) Scientists interpret this gas as emissions from hot magma below the regolith of Mars.

Although more research is required to confirm the emissions, the team suggested that Alba Mons may host an environment similar to hydrothermal vents on Earth, where life once likely arose and continues to thrive today.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances Wednesday (Nov. 4), is not the first to suggest that magma may be flowing on Mars; NASA's InSight lander interpreted its presence through seismic observations and modeling earlier this year. But the new findings are the strongest evidence yet of gases being released by dormant volcanoes on Mars, first study author Alexander Trokhimovskiy, at Russia's Space Research Institute, told Live Science.

"Our study offers a complementary and potentially independent line of evidence [of Martian magma]: Atmospheric observations that reveal a possible signature of gas release from a subsurface magmatic system," Trokhimovskiy wrote in an email.

TGO first detected hydrogen chloride gas in Mars' atmosphere in 2021, but scientists were hesitant to link it to volcanic activity. The gas appeared to be seasonal, its distribution was not localized at a possible volcanic region, and other signs of volcanic gases, like sulfur, were not present, study co-author Kevin Olsen, a visiting researcher at the University of Oxford who studies Mars gases, told Live Science in a separate email.

A photo of Mars with the Tharsis region centered.

Further work, however, suggested that the gas wasn't just popping up in the warmer spring and summer in Mars' southern hemisphere; it also appeared in the winter in the northern hemisphere, he noted.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"I managed to catch two observations from the start of northern winter in the first Mars year of our mission, and a single observation the next year," Olsen said, adding that a year on Mars is closer to two years on Earth due to the planet's wider orbit. "These out-of-season measurements were close to one another in location and time in both years, which was rather surprising. We then set about creating a campaign of special, targeted measurements at this time and place."

That campaign lasted two Mars years — roughly four Earth years — and increased the likelihood that scientists are seeing "an injection" of hydrogen chloride into the atmosphere from volcano-adjacent vents, Olsen said.

The scientists confirmed the unseasonal observations in the northern hemisphere, finding a "distinct and pronounced signal" that then diminishes and falls below the spacecraft's detection threshold. "This inconsistency is more suggestive of a puff of gas entering the atmosphere than of regular atmospheric chemistry," he said. "While the link remains a hypothesis, we have now seen this gas appear locally, and nowhere else, over four Mars years of observations."

Daniel Mège, also a co-author of the paper and a professor who studies planetary geology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, identified the fissures where the gas may be emerging. He said the complementary evidence from InSight (on the ground) and TGO (circling above) helps give the study weight: InSight spotted activity in the crust, while TGO detected the emissions in the atmosphere.

Although magma activity is not in itself a sign of life, Mège noted that Earth's first life-forms came from sites like hydrothermal zones, which have a similar confluence of materials and energy as the potential vents on Mars. But conditions would need to be favorable in that area for at least millions of years to allow life to form, he cautioned.

"If these requirements are met at local scale, at the scale of the seepage structures, then living organisms might wait for us to discover them," he told Live Science in an email. "But maintaining stable conditions over such a long period at a very local scale is not obvious."

#6228. NASA's Twin Spacecraft Will Execute Powered Slingshot Maneuvers on Their Way to Mars

A pair of NASA are spacecraft are about to perform a slingshot maneuver above Earth, and some of us might get to see them. They're on their way to Mars, where they'll dig more deeply into one of the Solar System's puzzles: how Mars lost its ancient atmosphere. The pair are unique, because once they reach the planet, they'll be the first spacecraft to "fly" in formation around Mars.

It's becoming clear, if not certain, that Mars was once warm and wet. It may have been habitable, even inhabited by simple life. But something happened and the planet is now cold and dead.

To be warm and wet, it must have had a much thicker atmosphere than the thin, CO2 atmosphere it has now. Scientists who study the iron-red world postulate that UV radiation from the Sun drove Mars' ancient atmosphere into space. That only happened after Mars' molten core cooled, and the planet lost its protective magnetic field. Once exposed to the full force of the Sun's UV radiation, the atmosphere was doomed.

Though its global magnetosphere is long gone, Mars still has patches of magnetic fields called crustal magnetic fields, or remnant magnetic fields. They aren't created by a dynamo; they're local magnetic fields generated by iron-rich chunks of the planet's crust. When Mars' dynamo failed billions of years ago, these chunks locked-in the magnetic orientation of the ancient crust. These surface fields on Mars also generate similar patches of magnetic fields in the planet's upper atmosphere. All these fields aren't anywere near as strong as the ancient dynamo, but they're enough to work with.

This map of Mars' crustal magnetism was created with data from NASA's now-defunct Mars Global Surveyor. In simple terms, it's a colour-coded map of the magnetic strength. Blue is weak, red is strong. Image Credit: By NASA - Public Domain.

While the broad picture of Mars' atmosphere loss is clear, the gritty details are not. The NASA spacecraft on their way to orbit Mars are called Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE). They're twins, named Red and Blue, and they'll measure how the solar wind interacts with the remnants of Mars' ancient magnetic field.

Soon the spacecraft will approach Earth. At their closest, they'll be between about 965 to 1,770 kilometers above the surface, and they'll use their thrusters to boost their speed. Those boosts will combined with Earth's gravity, and they'll slingshot their way to Mars. The first will do so on November 7th, the second on November 9th. These trans-Mars injection burns will last about 9 minutes and will increase their speed from about 10.14 km/s to 10.78 km/s. That's an increase of more than 2,000 km/hour.

These maneuvers are necessary because ESCAPADE didn't launch in the usual Mars launch window. Those windows occur about every 26 months. So the spacecraft had to loiter near the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 for a while, then approach Earth and use these burns to power their way to Mars. This led to some bonus science, where the spacecraft flew through and observed Earth's magnetotail. They were the first spacecraft to do so, and those observations will be shared soon.

A natural question arises about ESCAPADE: Why are there two spacecraft?

Solar wind interactions with magnetic fields can change on very short timescales. A single spacecraft wouldn't be able to tell if changes it observes are due to changes in these interactions, or changes in its position. A pair of spacecraft flying in formation removes this uncertainty. NASA calls this formation the "String of Pearls."

This animation shows the ESCAPADE spacecraft in their String of Pearls formation above Mars.

The spacecraft will fly the same orbit at varying distances from each other. But that's just for the first part of the mission, Science Phase A, which will last about 6 months. In Science Phase B, ESCAPADE's Blue and Red units will work more independently. Blue will lower its orbit to about 7,000 km and Red will raise its orbit to about 10,000 km. That will last about 5 months, until the end of ESCAPADE's nominal science mission. The spacecraft should remain in operation for many years after that, and NASA will have some decisions to make then.

The spacecraft will be visible to some observers on the ground, though a telescope will almost certainly be needed. They'll present as a pair of dim, refrigerator-sized objects moving against the starry background. Not super-exciting, but interesting nonetheless.

It's eerie to think about a planet like Mars losing its habitability and dying. It tells us something about the search for life, and about Earth. There may be multitudes of planets that were habitable for short periods of timeâmaybe hosting simple lifeâthat were extinguished before any complexity could arise. It puts life on Earth in perspective for its rarity. Earth has been habitable for billions of years, and, against probabilities, complex life has fluorished for hundreds of millions of years, even longer depending on which definition is used.

Having one of these extinguished planets next door is a rare opportunity to understand how this happens, and ESCAPADE will take full advantage of that opportunity.

#6227. Look Up: Three Meteor Showers, a Supermoon, and a Historic Space First Are Coming in November

November offers plenty of reasons to look up, including the Taurid and Leonid meteor showers, a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter, a remarkable milestone for NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, and a bright supermoon.

From shooting stars and planetary encounters to a spacecraft reaching an extraordinary distance from Earth, November is filled with celestial events worth watching. NASA’s latest skywatching guide highlights when and where to look for some of the month’s most interesting sights.

November begins with two opportunities to catch meteors streaking through the darkness. The Southern Taurids reach their peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids approximately one week later, around November 12.

Both showers take their names from the constellation Taurus. Although the meteors travel across different parts of the sky, they appear to originate from two distinct regions within this constellation.

Neither shower is particularly active compared with some of the year’s bigger meteor displays. Under ideal conditions, each typically produces about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally generating exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The next major meteor display arrives later in the month, when the Leonids become the focus of attention.

For the best chance of seeing them, head outside during the early morning hours of November 17 or 18, once the Moon has dropped below the horizon. With favorable conditions, observers could see as many as 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

A few simple preparations can make a significant difference. Choose a viewing location away from bright city lights, allow approximately 30 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness, and find a comfortable position that gives you a broad view of the sky.

Meteor showers are not the only attraction this November. Two of the solar system’s most recognizable planets will also put on an impressive display.

Before sunrise on November 15 and 16, look toward the southeastern sky to find Mars and Jupiter appearing remarkably close together.

The planets will be separated by approximately 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the combined apparent width of two full Moons. Jupiter will stand out as the brighter object, while Mars will be visible nearby with its distinctive reddish color.

No telescope or binoculars are required to enjoy the pairing, since both planets can be seen with the naked eye. Although they remain separated by enormous distances in space, their positions relative to Earth make them appear close together in our sky.

Observers who check their positions over several consecutive mornings can watch the two planets gradually approach one another before appearing to move apart again.

Far beyond the planets visible in November’s morning sky, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching an unprecedented achievement.

During November, Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. This means the spacecraft will be so far away that even a signal traveling at the speed of light will need 24 hours to reach it.

Receiving a response will require another 24 hours, bringing the total communication time for a signal and its reply to approximately two full days.

The spacecraft is much too distant to be seen, but skywatchers can get a sense of its direction by locating Ophiuchus, the constellation also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling in that general direction as it continues its journey into interstellar space.

To recognize this historic achievement, NASA is inviting the public to participate in its Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation on November 17.

The month concludes with another eye-catching event when a full supermoon rises on November 24.

The Moon does not travel around Earth in a perfectly circular orbit. Instead, its slightly elliptical path causes its distance from our planet to vary throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs while the Moon is relatively close to Earth, it is commonly called a supermoon. From our perspective, it appears somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon, although the visual difference is often difficult to notice.

November’s supermoon is particularly notable because it marks the beginning of three consecutive months featuring supermoons, with additional events arriving in December and January.

For a memorable view, look toward the eastern horizon around sunset as the full Moon begins to rise. It may seem enormous when positioned close to the horizon, but this apparent increase in size is largely caused by a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

The effect can occur with any full Moon, regardless of its actual distance from Earth, making November’s moonrise an especially appealing opportunity to experience it.

Moon phases for November 2026, showing the dates for Third Quarter, New Moon, First Quarter, Full “Supermoon,” and a concluding Third Quarter in Pacific Time. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
