#6225. The ELT Can Probe Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies and Their Dark Matter Mysteries

We've been waiting a long time for the Extremely Large Telescope's first light, scheduled for March 2029. Telescopes this large, powerful, and costly always have multiple science goals, and that's true for the ELT. One of its science goals is to study fundamental aspects of the Universe, including dark matter.

The current model of cosmology is called Lambda Cold Dark Matter (Lambda-CDM or ÎCDM.) It's basically the Big Bang model of cosmology. There are, as every space-head knows, unanswered questions about Lambda-CDM, including the fact that we don't even know what dark matter is. (Some don't think it even exists.)

This is where the ELT comes in. One of its proposed instruments, and telescopes like this always have multiple instruments attached, is called NEXUS@SHARP. SHARP stands for Spectrograph for High Angular Resolution Physics, and NEXUS is a Multi-Object Spectrograph designed to work with SHARP.

New research in the journal New Astronomy outlines how NEXUS@SHARP can probe questions about Lambda-CDM. It's titled "SHARP(ening the) view of unresolved globular clusters in ultra diffuse galaxies," and the lead author is Marco Mirabile. Mirabile is a PhD student at INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Abruzzo (INAF-OAAb) and Gran Sasso Science institute (GSSI) in Italy.

"Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies (UDGs) challenge current galaxy formation models within the ÎCDM framework, particularly regarding their dark matter content and formation histories," the authors write. "Globular Clusters (GCs) serve as excellent tracers for probing the halos of these faint systems; however, current spectroscopic facilities struggle to reach the depth required to fully characterize GC populations beyond the local neighborhood."

UDGs are unusual because they're about as large as the Milky Way, but can have thousands of times fewer stars. The stars are spread out and the galaxies are dim. Basically they're too puffy to agree with Lambda-CDM.

This visualization shows how stars are distributed in a simulated UDG. UDGs are as faint as dwarf galaxies, but are spread out like large galaxies like the Milky Way. Astronomers thought that supernovae explosions could've been responsible for spreading out the stars, but that interpretation hasn't endured. Image Credit: Arianna Di Cintio, Chris Brook, NIHAO simulations and HST

A galaxy's size is shaped by its dark matter halo, one of the cosmos' basic structural units. There's an apparent mismatch between the sizes of UDG halos and the sizes of the UDGs themselves. The expected size of the halos shouldn't produce such diffuse galaxies.

A way to understand this is to examine the globular clusters around UDGs. But the problem is, the spectroscopes astronomers have at their disposal now aren't powerful enough to fully characterize the globular clusters around UDGs. NEXUS@SHARP can extend their reach.

"In this work, we present the scientific potential of NEXUS@SHARP, a near-infrared multi-slit spectrograph proposed on the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). We demonstrate that NEXUS is uniquely positioned to overcome current observational limitations by combining high spatial resolution with efficient multiplexing," the authors write. Multiplexing means it's a Multi-Object Spectrograph (MOS) that can observe and capture data from many GCs at once. MOSs are common; Keck, the VLT, Gemini, and the JWST all have them, so do many others. But NEXUS@SHARP would be attached to the extraordinarly powerful ELT and its 39.3-metre-diameter segmented mirror.

All galaxies have globular clusters, including our own. Globular clusters are important when studying UDGs because they're brighter than the UDGs that hosts them, and are easier to observe. They also extend outward further than the UDGs, so they can help measure the dark matter halo better. That should let astronomers measure a more accurate mass constraint. Not only that, but the number of GCs can help determine the mass of the halo because their number scales with mass.

Omega Centauri, seen in this image captured with the WFI camera from ESO's La Silla Observatory, is probably the most well-known of the Milky Way's globular clusters. It has as many as 10 million stars. GCs are bright, so when they're satellites of ultra-diffuse galaxies, they serve as good probes of the galaxies. Image Credit: ESO

Another important thing GC spectra tells scientists is their formation history. The spectra show the ages and the metallicities of GCs, which reveals how quickly the stars in the GC formed. That can show astronomers what kind of UDG they're looking at.

Measuring a handful of GCs around a small number of UDGs won't sufficiently characterize the population of either. NEXUS@SHARP will bring more of them within observational rearch, and it won't require much telescope time because NEXUS examines many GCs at once. "We show that NEXUS can efficiently help to characterize the GC population in UDGs across diverse environments â out to 60 to 70 Mpc â with a few hours of ELT time," the authors write. 70 megaparsecs is about 230 light years.

The ELT is a beast of a telescope, and its heart is the 39.3 meter segmented primary mirror. Its instruments, including NEXUS@SHARP if its built, sit on a separate stationary platform. Image Credit: ESO

What this boils down to is two different scenarios for how UDGs form, and what it tells astronomers about dark matter and Lambda-CDM.

"These capabilities will allow for precise measurements of radial velocities and stellar populations, enabling robust dynamical mass estimates and distinguishing between competing UDG formation scenarios," the authors write.

One scenario says that UDGs are failed massive galaxies that were quenched early on. These ones preserved their dwarf-like stellar masses, but lie within more massive halos typical of a regular galaxy. "These galaxies would thus appear red, old, metal-poor, DM dominated, and host unusually rich globular cluster (GC) populations," the authors write.

The second says that UDGs are puffed-up dwarfs. They are genuinely low-mass galaxies that have expanded in space for some reason. "Relative to the previous scenario, such objects are expected to be bluer, exhibit extended star formation histories, and have DM content and GC populations resembling those of typical dwarfs," the authors explain.

NEXUS@SHARP can shed light on these scenarios and help explain how UDGs formed by examining globular clusters around Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies. That's why the authors wrote that ""Globular Clusters (GCs) serve as excellent tracers for probing the halos of these faint systems."

"To shed light on the nature of UDGs, deep spectroscopic observations of a large sample of UDGs are needed, as combining the analysis of GC richness with the kinematic and evolutionary properties of field stars provides a powerful diagnostic for distinguishing between different formation channels," the authors write.

Basically, the dataset gathered by NEXUS@SHARP will have two independent mass measurements for each UDG, both arising from measuring many GCs at once. One mass measurement comes from the velocity dispersion of the GCs, which shows how much mass is required to keep them in orbit. That's dynamical mass.

The second is also from GCs, but measures their total number. That relies on the knowledge that the number of GCs roughly rises linearly with the mass of a UDG's dark matter halo. That's GC-count mass.

This figure from previous research shows how the number of globular clusters (y-axis) correlates with galaxy mass (x-axis). Each orange or blue circle represents the number of GCs in an individual galaxy. Image Credit: Minh Ngoc Le and Andrew P. Cooper 2025 ApJ 978 33

If both of these ways of measuring mass agree, and both are high, that means that the UDG has an overmassive halo compared to its number of stars. That supports the first UDG formation scenario: it's a failed regular galaxy that quenched early.

If the different measurements both agree, but they're low, that supports the second UDG formation scenario: it's a puffed up dwarf inside a normal sized dwarf dark matter halo.

There's another wrinkle. If the dynamical mass is low, but the GC-count mass is high, then the formation of GC was unusually inefficient for some other, environmental reason.

NEXUS@SHARP is just a concept at this point, and the paper just makes the case for building it. If it's built, the results could go a long way to a better understanding of dark matter and Lambda-CDM. Understanding Lambda-CDM is an ongoing effort, and it's being tackled from different directions with different facilities. While Lambda-CDM is still the best match for lots of data about dark matter and dark energy, it doesn't fit everything.

If built, NEXUS@SHARP can chip away at some of the uncertainty around Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies and their dark matter halos, and can help either confirm or contradict Lambda-CDM.

"By enabling the systematic spectroscopic survey of GCs in low-surface-brightness systems, NEXUS@SHARP will act as a definitive tool for constraining the formation channels of the most elusive galaxy populations in the local universe," the authors conclude.

#6224. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6223. NASA’s Perseverance Mars Rover Just Drove Farther Than Any Vehicle Beyond Earth

NASA’s self-driving Perseverance rover has broken the all-time off-world driving record and is now exploring ancient Martian terrain that could hold clues to the Red Planet’s long-lost history.

NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for driving on another world, traveling farther across the surface of Mars than any vehicle in history. On October 11, its total distance reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), surpassing the previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) held by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which operated on Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance achieved the milestone on its 2,006th Martian day, known as a sol, completing in just five and a half years a journey that took Opportunity nearly 15.

The record was broken as Perseverance made its way toward a location called “Idubi,” passing through an area nicknamed “Lac de Charmes” just beyond the western edge of Jezero Crater. Scientists believe this region contains some of the most ancient terrain ever investigated in the solar system. Comparable rocks on Earth have largely disappeared because of erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates). At Idubi, researchers hope to uncover evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, where hot water once interacted with surrounding rock.

A major reason Perseverance has been able to travel so far is its sophisticated autonomous driving technology. Its navigation system, called AutoNav, allows the rover to analyze its surroundings and choose a safe route while moving. As it drives, Perseverance captures images, creates three-dimensional maps of potential obstacles, and determines how to travel between destinations chosen by engineers on Earth. NASA describes this ability as “thinking while driving.”

Unlike earlier rovers, Perseverance can perform these calculations while traveling at or close to its maximum speed. It has covered as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single Martian day. More than 90% of its total driving distance has involved AutoNav evaluating the terrain, a dramatic improvement over the roughly 5% achieved by the first Martian AutoNav system used by Opportunity and its twin rover, Spirit.

The difference in computing capability is equally remarkable. NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, relied on just 20 measurement points to evaluate the ground ahead. Perseverance now analyzes 600,000 points every time it examines the terrain.

“It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,” said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.”

NASA has already authorized the first extension of the Perseverance mission. The extended phase began in October and is expected to keep the rover investigating the rim of Jezero Crater through approximately the end of 2028.

Perseverance’s accomplishment builds on nearly three decades of robotic exploration on Mars. With each new generation, NASA has developed rovers capable of traveling greater distances and navigating increasingly challenging landscapes.

The journey began in 1997 with Sojourner, a small rover roughly the size of a microwave oven. During its 83-sol mission, it traveled approximately 330 feet (100 meters). In 2004, NASA sent the much larger, golf-cart-sized rovers Spirit and Opportunity to Mars. Although both were originally designed for missions lasting just 90 sols, they went on to far exceed expectations.

Spirit traveled 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) before its mission ended during the harsh Martian winter of 2010. Opportunity proved even more durable, operating for 5,111 sols and completing the first marathon-distance drive on another world in 2015. Its extraordinary journey established the distance record that Perseverance has now broken.

NASA’s Curiosity rover, which arrived at Gale Crater in 2012 and continues exploring Mars, has accumulated more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers) of driving.

Perseverance is not simply traveling farther than its predecessors. Its ability to navigate independently has continued to improve since it landed on Mars.

“The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,” Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance. “Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive. The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the Sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.”

Before surpassing Opportunity’s Mars record, Perseverance had already traveled farther than vehicles driven on the Moon. Its journey exceeded the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972, as well as the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) traveled by the Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.

These achievements demonstrate how much robotic mobility has advanced, but setting records is not the mission’s primary objective. The real advantage of traveling farther and faster is that scientists can investigate more locations, examine a wider variety of rocks, and piece together a more complete picture of Mars’ ancient history.

Perseverance’s growing range has allowed it to explore several dramatically different Martian environments. Its journey began on the floor of an ancient lake, continued through the remains of a long-vanished river system, and eventually brought it to the rim of Jezero Crater.

Along the way, the rover discovered a rock called “Cheyava Falls” containing a potential biosignature, a feature that could provide evidence of ancient biological activity. Scientists are now investigating another type of environment that may once have offered conditions suitable for life: hydrothermal systems associated with heated water and rock.

So far, Perseverance has gathered 29 samples of rock and regolith, the loose material covering the Martian surface. These samples represent several distinct geological settings, including the crater floor, a delta formed by an ancient river, and the surrounding crater rim.

Near the rim, the rover has been studying rocks formed or altered by powerful impacts roughly 4 billion years ago. These formations preserve evidence from an extremely early period of planetary history, much of which has been destroyed or transformed by geological processes on Earth.

After completing its investigation of Lac de Charmes, Perseverance is expected to continue following the crater rim before turning south during its extended mission. One of its destinations is Rainbow Falls, an enormous block of ancient crust measuring 328 feet (100 meters) across that was pushed upward by the impact responsible for creating Jezero Crater.

With its driving systems still functioning and years of additional exploration planned, Perseverance is positioned to keep extending its record while uncovering new clues about the Red Planet’s distant past.

A Roman-era belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest hints at the ancient conflict between the Romans and the Dacians.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

#6220. Our Sun’s Undiscovered Stellar Nemesis Is Still Out There, Says Physicist

Long period, high inclination comets of the sort that can cause extinction level impacts here on Earth have long been thought to originate from a theoretical Oort Cloud. That is, a roughly spherical cloud of icy cometary objects that number into the trillions at distances that extend up to 1.6 light years away.

More recently, Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California Berkeley, put forth the idea that long period comets that visit our inner solar system are not just caused by passing stars perturbing the outer edges of the Oort Cloud. But they are also perturbed by a low mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) that along with our Sun is orbiting around a common center of gravity.

Due to Nemesisâ slightly eccentric oval orbit around the Oort Cloud, it periodically perturbs billions of comets that surround our outer solar system.

Every time Nemesis gets closest to the Oort Cloud is when the comets kick in and this comet shower lasts for maybe a million years, Muller told me via phone. That's when Nemesis is in the densest part of the comet cloud, and that's when the number of deflected Oort Cloud comets into the inner solar system are at a maximum, he says.

Just to be clear, this is not any sort of Planet X. This also doesnât have anything to do with random stellar interlopers that sometimes pass close enough to perturb our Oort Cloud and stir up a plethora of inward bound comets.

In contrast, there is nothing random about Nemesis. This is a phenomenon with a clear periodicity. According to Muller, itâs responsible for 250 million years of clearly defined periodic Earth impacts.

In a 1982 paper in the journal Science, two paleontologists, David Raup and Jack Sepkoski, collected the most extensive record of marine extinctions ever and if you plot those extinctions, you see there's a strong 26-million-year period in the data, says Muller.

The mysterious and hypothetical Oort Cloud is thought to be the home of long-period comets that visit the inner Solar System. Image Credit: ESA. LICENCE: ESA Standard Licence

One of the peaks was at 66 million years ago, the KT boundary extinction which wiped out the dinosaurs.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. I said, "Well, maybe there's a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth," he says.

It's an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn't sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, says Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of Franceâs Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email. Planetesimals that originated in our Sun's planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun's birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he says.

Why hasnât Nemesis already been directly detected?

Many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because itâs moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesnât show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be big enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means itâs probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, says Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

Yet the evidence that it's an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that's what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, "You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?" He said, "Sure, we couldn't tell the difference."

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, says Muller.

The bad news is that if it's out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie co-planar to most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, says Muller.

#6219. NASA Space Telescope Meets Fiery End After Nearly 22 Years in Orbit

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary mission of cosmic discovery to an end. The spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, more than two decades after launching in 2004.

Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes capable of detecting different wavelengths of light. It was the first observatory of its kind, built to investigate some of the most powerful explosions in the universe.

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on November 4, above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere, although some pieces may have survived the descent.

When Swift launched in 2004, its primary goal was to study gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily energetic explosions that rank among the most powerful events in the cosmos. The observatory was initially expected to operate for just two years, but it continued collecting valuable scientific data for more than two decades.

Over its remarkable lifetime, Swift became an exceptionally versatile tool for astronomers. Its instruments could observe several types of light, allowing researchers to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena. The spacecraft could also quickly turn toward sudden, short-lived bursts of energy and notify other observatories, giving scientists an opportunity to study events that might otherwise disappear before they could be examined.

These capabilities helped transform our understanding of the universe. Swift contributed to discoveries involving active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars producing powerful X-ray flares, and the spectacular explosions of dying stars known as supernovas. Its observations also extended much closer to home, providing valuable information about comets and asteroids traveling through our own solar system.

What began as a two-year mission ultimately became nearly 22 years of exploring the universe, leaving behind a remarkable scientific legacy.

#6217. Could a Nasal Spray Stop Alzheimer’s Before Memory Loss Begins?

Protecting memory from Alzheimer’s may one day involve a nasal spray, with encouraging results in animals and evidence that its particles also protect human neurons grown in the lab.

Alzheimer’s disease damages the connections that allow brain cells to communicate, threatening memory. A nasal spray containing tiny particles naturally released by cells has helped protect those connections in an animal model of the disease. The treatment both prevented memory deficits and countered cognitive decline after it had begun.

The particles, called extracellular vesicles, are small packages that cells release into their surroundings. Those used in this study came from cells of the amniotic membrane, the tissue lining the sac that surrounds a developing fetus. Researchers at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, and the E. Menni Research Center of Fondazione Poliambulanza reported the findings in Translational Neurodegeneration.

When administered through the nose to animals that mimic features of Alzheimer’s disease, the vesicles reached the hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory and particularly vulnerable to the disease. There, they entered both neurons and microglia, cells that monitor conditions in the brain and help defend it. The treatment counteracted neuroinflammation and protected neuronal function, particularly at synapses, the connections through which nerve cells transmit information. These effects were accompanied by a significant improvement in cognitive abilities.

The choice of amniotic membrane cells grew out of years of placental research by Professor Ornella Parolini, a full professor of applied biology and scientific director of IRCCS Ospedale “Casa Sollievo della sofferenza.” Her work has focused on these cells and the substances they release, collectively known as the secretome, investigating their protective and regenerative effects in various experimental models. The E. Menni Research Center, led by Parolini, contributed expertise in isolating and characterizing the cells and identifying the molecules they produce.

The research combined the expertise of Professor Claudio Grassi, whose team at the Università Cattolica studies brain inflammation and plasticity, with work by Professor Salvatore Fusco on the vesicles’ effects in the brain. Lead authors Dr. Andrea Papait and Dr. Francesca Natale helped connect these findings, investigating how amniotic extracellular vesicles influence brain inflammation, neuronal function, and memory.

The findings also suggest that effective Alzheimer’s treatments may need to address more than the buildup of harmful proteins in the brain.

Professor Fusco explains: “The study suggests the need to direct research into Alzheimer’s therapies by focusing not only on counteracting the accumulation of toxic compounds like beta-amyloid and tau, but also by paying close attention to the cellular environment in which neurons live (e.g., microglia and astrocytes) and the molecular signals (e.g., cytokines or microRNAs) exchanged by these cells, which can influence synapse function.”

To investigate the protective effects in human cells, researchers used skin biopsies collected from patients with Alzheimer’s disease and healthy individuals at the Policlinico’s Memory Clinic. From those samples, they generated pluripotent stem cells, which can develop into different cell types, and then used those cells to produce human neurons.

The vesicles also showed protective effects in these laboratory-grown neurons, extending the evidence to experimental human models and giving the study a closer connection to patients.

Professor Grassi emphasizes that the findings are encouraging but still preliminary.

“These are preclinical results that require further validation in humans and do not yet represent an available therapy for Alzheimer’s disease, but they point to a very promising direction: understanding whether some of the mechanisms through which the placenta naturally regulates inflammation and protects tissues could offer new tools for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases and, more generally, whether the use of extracellular vesicles represents a new frontier for the treatment of neurological diseases.”

Reference: “Human amniotic mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles reprogram microglia and prevent neurodegeneration in experimental models of Alzheimer’s disease” by Andrea Papait, Francesca Natale, Antonietta Rosa Silini, Ida Nifo Sarrapochiello, Elisa Orecchini, Raimondo Sollazzo, Marco Rinaudo, Serafina Farigu, Nicoletta Garofalo, Giulia Mantini, Guido Maria Giuffrè, Pietro Romele, Elvira Ragozzino, Alice Dellaria, Luciano Giacò, Camillo Marra, Cristian Ripoli, Claudio Grassi, Ornella Parolini and Salvatore Fusco, 9 September 2026, Translational neurodegeneration. DOI: 10.1186/s40035-026-00581-1

#6216. NASA’s Swift telescope faced a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s tenure has ended, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. On November 4, Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere, where it was expected to burn up. This fiery end capped an uncontrollable fall from space.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift was doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6214. A New Fiber Supplement Could Be a Game Changer for Millions With IBS

For people with IBS, a specially designed fiber blend could support a healthier gut without added pain or bloating, a trial alongside a low-FODMAP diet suggests.

Cutting out foods that leave you bloated or in pain can bring welcome relief. For millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome, or IBS, however, a diet that eases discomfort can come with a trade-off. Restricting certain foods can also reduce fiber intake and the beneficial bacteria that help support gut health.

Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) in Australia have tested a specially formulated fiber blend that could help address that dilemma. Called ur gut, the supplement combines high-amylose maize resistant starch with psyllium husk powder. In a small clinical trial, the blend changed the composition of participants’ gut bacteria without worsening their abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

IBS is common worldwide and affects nearly 11 percent of Australians. Its cause remains unknown, although stress, infection, and medication are potential triggers. Certain foods, poor sleep, psychological stress, hormonal fluctuations, and lifestyle factors can aggravate symptoms.

One common recommendation is a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that gut bacteria readily ferment.

“For years we’ve known that a diet low in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time,” said lead author Dr. Tina Yan.

“We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.”

Scientists at ECU’s Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) developed the blend and trialed it in people with IBS who were following a low-FODMAP diet. Adding fiber in this setting requires care because bacteria can produce gas as they break it down.

“Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort,” Dr. Yan said.

“What’s exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.”

The changes in participants’ gut bacterial composition were significant, and their extent stood out to ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine.

“Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention,” she said.

“The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.”

The researchers suspect the explanation lies in how the blend’s two ingredients, resistant starch and psyllium husk, work together. Resistant starch escapes digestion in the small intestine, leaving it available for bacteria to ferment in the colon. Psyllium appears to slow that fermentation, allowing the starch to travel farther into the colon before bacteria break it down. The researchers believe this enhances the production of beneficial metabolites, substances the bacteria produce as they process the starch.

“For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods,” said ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen.

“Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That’s an important step forward.”

Reference: “Dietary fiber blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomized, double-blind control trial” by Ran Yan, Amanda Devine, Johnny Lo, Evania Marlow, Ian C. Dunican, Kanita Kunaratnam, Lesley Andrew and Claus T. Christophersen, 24 September 2026, European Journal of Nutrition. DOI: 10.1007/s00394-026-04113-5

#6213. A 400-Year-Old Mass Murderer Led a Brutal Mutiny—and Became the First Corporate Psychopath

A modern psychopathy test, applied to a 1629 shipwreck, uncovers the dark origins of toxic bosses.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When you try to envision a “corporate psychopath,” the kind of individual who blends charm towards their superiors and sadism towards their subordinates to rise through the corporate ranks, who comes to mind?

Actually, don’t say a specific name. These guys can be very litigious, so let’s just focus on the vague and the deceased. You’re probably picturing a man in an expensive business suit, maybe having a loud, hyperbolic conversation on an oversized 1980s cell phone. Maybe he’s monologuing about how “greed is good,” or how they’re “gonna need to send the National Guard to take him out, ‘cause he’s not goin’ nowhere.” Perhaps the corporate psychopath you have in mind is busy fretting about whether his business card has lettering in Romalian or Silian Rail.

In other words, short of someone you’ve seen on the news, or in your own boardroom, your mental image of a corporate psychopath probably comes from the movies.

You may want to revise that. That’s because a new study suggests that the original corporate psycho predates the 1980s stock market antiheroes of the movies you love. He actually predates movies entirely. In fact, he died before the city of Boston was ever founded.

In a study published in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics, Clive Roland Boddy, an author and pioneer in the study of corporate psychopathy, has identified Jeronimous Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Company as perhaps the earliest documented example of a corporate psychopath. To understand why, one must delve into the dark story of the 1629 Batavia shipwreck and its mutinous aftermath.

The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, translated as Dutch East India Company and abbreviated as VOC, was a fairly unique venture in the business world at the dawn of the 17th century. At the time, expeditions for goods and resources were often funded individually, and the companies behind them lasted only as long as a single voyage. The VOC changed that by merging 12 existing “pre-companies” within the Dutch Republic into a permanent company that would not only fund spice expeditions but also manage supply and stabilize the market. Shares of the VOC could be publicly purchased and traded by Dutch citizens at various aftermarkets throughout the Republic, including the predecessor to the Euronext Amsterdam, arguably making the VOC the world’s first multinational corporation.

In some ways, the VOC resembled the multinational corporations we know today, with the same ruthless efficiency. Yet the world around it lacked the kind of laws and regulations that are at least supposed to keep the corporations of our modern world in check. In fact, the Dutch government backed the VOC entirely, allowing the company to have a monopoly over the Asian spice trade. It was an environment that favored the bold, the ambitious, and the unscrupulous. It was an environment that allowed a man like Jeronimus Cornelisz to seize his moment.

“Psychopaths have a narcissistic and grossly inflated view of their self-worth and importance,” Mike Dash writes in his book Batavia’s Graveyard: The True Story of the Mad Heretic Who Led History’s Bloodiest Mutiny, “...a truly astonishing egocentricity and sense of entitlement, and see themselves as the centre of the universe, as superior beings who are justified in living according to their own rules.” It’s unclear exactly when Jeronimus Cornelisz created his own set of rules to live by, whether in his poorly-documented childhood, or when he took up his apothecary trade some time in the 1620s and began battling with his local town council.

What we know is that by 1628, the death of his child and the subsequent scandal it invited (the three-month old had died of syphilis, and Cornelisz tried to argue the child had contracted it from a wet nurse rather than his own wife) led to the Dutchman selling his business and taking a job with the VOC. In October 1628, the Batavia left port in the Netherlands on a trip to the Dutch East Indies, with commodore Francisco Pelsaert as its commander, Ariaen Jacobsz as its skipper, and Cornelisz as a junior officer.

Pelsaert’s journal recounts that on June 4, 1629, “I was lying in my bunk feeling ill and felt suddenly, with a rough terrible movement, the bumping of the ship’s rudder, and immediately after that I felt the ship held up in her course against the rocks, so that I fell out of my bunk.” The vessel had run aground on Western Australia’s Morning Reef while Jacobsz was at the helm, and roughly 100 of the 340 people aboard the ship were killed in the collision. To date, there’s still fierce debate over whether the Batavia crashed “by design or accident,” as by this time, Cornelisz had charmed his way into Jacobsz’ esteem, and in doing so, had convinced him that a mutiny was necessary to depose Pelsaert.

Either way, as some of the roughly 180 survivors disembarked for the nearby islands, leaving only 70 (including Cornelisz) aboard, an opportunity arose for the original “hostile takeover.”

Cornelisz had originally been among the 70 or so who remained aboard the Batavia, but after nine days, he made his way to nearby Beacon Island. He found the survivors stranded there to be starving, dying of thirst, and feeling abandoned, since Pelsaert had left with the other officers in search of supplies and aid. Seizing his moment, Cornelisz stepped into the leadership vacuum, amassing a group of loyal enforcers, and stripping the now subordinate survivors of any means by which to fend for, or defend, themselves.

Cornelisz began a reign of terror that lasted more than two months, overseeing the execution of those deemed “too weak,” as well as those he thought capable of overpowering him. Supplies were hoarded for his loyalists, while those outside of his circle were dispatched in ever more public and brutal ways. His roughly 40 man cadre killed an estimated 100-125 men, women, and children, and the survivors didn’t fare much better.

“Furthermore, when the most murders had been committed,” Pelseart would write in his journal, “...they shared the women who remained, or rather whom they had meant to stay alive.” Cornelisz, who had singled out Lucretia Jansz for his own ill-intent, “made several articles to which the women had to be put on oath if they wanted to remain alive, that they had to be obedient to the men in all that they should desire of them.”

While all of this may read like the barbaric horrors of a bygone age, befitting a pirate’s pillaging more than a modern boardroom, Boddy’s study found that when Cornelisz’s actions are viewed through the prism of The Psychopathy Measure–Management Research Version (PM–MRV), a ten-item model he previously developed to identify contemporary corporate psychopaths, the mutinous, murderous junior officer of the VOC checked off every box.

Boddy’s article doesn’t recontextualize Cornelisz’s crimes to exonerate the man; there’s little debate that Jeronimus was a psychopath of some stripe. Nor does Boddy suggest that the existence of the VOC created or caused Cornelisz’s monstrous urges. Rather, it emphasizes that the profit motive built into the structure of the VOC “would have been too great, even for a careful primary psychopath” to resist. This analysis demonstrates that corporate psychopaths as we know them today “have been active since the start of the World’s first stock exchange, and first multinational shareholder-owned corporations.” What unites Cornelisz with the less-overtly-murderous corporate psychopaths we encounter today is the manner in which they both “utilise a similar modus operandi across the centuries and are motivated by greed, self-aggrandisement, and the desire to hurt, dominate and control others.”

In other words, to subvert a quote lamented by another lunatic, Billy Loomis in 1996’s Scream: corporations don’t create psychos. Corporations make psychos more creative.

#6212. Scientists Discover a Hidden Eye Disease That Can Steal Your Night Vision

Researchers can spot signs of a newly identified genetic eye disease before light-sensing cells are lost by measuring how vision recovers in darkness.

People with a newly identified genetic eye condition can see well for most of their lives before gradually losing peripheral vision and struggling to see at dusk or at night. The condition is linked to a gene already associated with a different eye disease, one that affects central vision first.

The two conditions arise from different variants, or versions, of the EFEMP1 gene. The newly identified variant, p.Arg140Trp, causes abnormally thick material to build up between cells in the eye. Researchers are calling the condition EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration, or L-ORD, although it has not been formally named.

L-ORD begins slowly at the periphery of the retina, the tissue at the back of the eye that converts light into signals the brain interprets as sight. Its gradual progression makes it difficult to detect. One useful clue is unusually slow recovery of vision when a person moves from a lighted setting into low light. This adjustment involves rod photoreceptors, the retinal cells specialized for seeing in dim conditions.

“We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact,” said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.”

The investigation began with a clinical description of a family in the United States in 1998.

“The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found,” Cideciyan said. “Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.”

The genetic finding allowed researchers to expand the investigation to multiple European families. They studied three unrelated families in different countries that shared the p.Arg140Trp variant and compared them with a separate family carrying p.Arg345Trp, the EFEMP1 variant responsible for the already-known condition affecting central vision.

Published in JAMA Ophthalmology, the research involved an international team that included scientists from the Scheie Eye Institute of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. Researchers from the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn also contributed.

The researchers do not yet know how widespread p.Arg140Trp is or how many people have this form of L-ORD. They suspect it may be relatively rare, but larger studies are needed to establish its prevalence.

“Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging,” said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.”

Reference: “Widening the Spectrum of Disease Expression due to Heterozygous Variants in EFEMP1” by Chloe M. Stanton, Georg Ansari, Kristina Pfau, Theresa Lipsky, Mihail Halachev, Lukas Gerasimavicius, Camilla Drake, Joseph A. Marsh, Caroline Hayward, Alexander Sumaroka, Bohdan Kousal, Petra Lišková, Mathieu Quinodoz, Carlo Rivolta, Tomas S. Aleman, Artur V. Cideciyan and Maximilian Pfau, 10 September 2026, JAMA Ophthalmology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2026.3828

This study was supported by grants from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor’s Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

#6210. Einstein Was Right Again: Scientists Discover Chemical Bonds That Defy Textbook Rules

Scientists have uncovered direct evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes how atoms form triple chemical bonds in heavy elements.

A fundamental rule of chemical bonding begins to break down when atoms become sufficiently heavy. Chemists at Brown University have found direct experimental evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes the structure of triple bonds, challenging a model that has been taught in chemistry classrooms for generations.

The discovery, published in Science, comes from experiments involving carbon and bismuth, a heavy element whose electrons are strongly influenced by relativistic effects. “This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s,” said Lai-Sheng Wang, a Brown chemistry professor and the study’s corresponding author. “But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn’t true in heavy elements.”

Chemical bonds form when atoms share electrons, creating an attraction that holds their positively charged nuclei together. In the conventional description of a triple bond, three shared electron pairs produce one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The sigma bond forms through direct overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, while the pi bonds involve electron density extending to either side of that axis.

This arrangement accurately describes many bonds involving lighter elements. In heavier atoms, however, the strong positive charge of the nucleus causes some electrons to move at speeds where relativistic effects become significant. These effects strengthen a phenomenon called spin-orbit coupling, which links an electron’s spin to its orbital motion and changes how electrons participate in bonding.

“The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared,” Wang said. “We still have three bonds, but we don’t really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.”

To investigate this effect, Brown doctoral students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, working with Wang and their colleagues, produced molecules containing carbon and bismuth. They cooled the molecules to temperatures near absolute zero before examining them with photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses light to eject electrons and measures their energies to determine how strongly they were bound.

The resulting spectra provided evidence of a triple bond unlike the conventional arrangement. Instead of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth bond exhibited characteristics consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds. This experimentally observed structure supports theoretical predictions that relativistic spin-orbit coupling can fundamentally alter bonding in heavy elements.

The findings could influence how chemists describe bonds involving heavy elements, particularly as researchers explore their potential in advanced technologies. Bismuth has attracted attention as a possible alternative to toxic lead in next-generation solar cells. It is also being investigated in quantum materials and research relevant to quantum computing.

Understanding how relativistic effects influence its chemical bonds may help scientists develop more accurate descriptions of bismuth-containing compounds and other heavy-element materials. The new evidence could eventually change how these bonds are presented in chemistry textbooks.

“Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements,” Wang said.

Reference: “Relativistic collapse of the classical triple bond in the CBi− molecular ion” by Deniz Kahraman, Jie Hui, Xin-Yu Zhang, Neil A. Ellis, Hyun Wook Choi, Kirk A. Peterson and Lai-Sheng Wang, 9 July 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aei1285

The work was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

Wang, S. (2026). A mid-Cretaceous island as a cradle of Southeast Asian plant biodiversity. Nature Ecology & Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-026-03219-7
